title: Labor inquiry says new defence laws could have significant human rights impact
content:
A Labor‑chaired inquiry warned that new defence legislation granting officials the authority to use lethal force against suspected trespassers in designated zones could have “significant” human‑rights implications. The committee highlighted the absence of requirements to provide detained individuals with fresh drinking water or humane conditions, and cautioned that the broad changes might affect members of the public who inadvertently enter a defence security zone that has not been publicised.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese defended the laws, describing criticism of them as “nonsense” and “conspiracy theories” from the far left and far right.
summary: Labor inquiry says new defence laws could have significant human rights impact.
author: Guardian World

title: Senate inquiry says Labor's Support at Home program leaves older Australians without care
content: The Support at Home system has ‘baffling’ bureaucracy and ‘rations and denies care’, says Greens chair of Senate inquiry Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast Many older Australians are dying before they can access home support, paying exorbitant fees, and being pushed into hospitals and residential care before they are ready because of a flawed federal government aged care program, a Senate inquiry has found. The inquiry is examining the impact of the Support at Home program, which launched in November 2025 and has been plagued by complaints of making care harder to access and more expensive. The inquiry was due to finish in November, but has been extended for a further year after receiving almost 300 submissions.
summary: The Senate inquiry found that the federal Support at Home program, launched in November 2025, is plagued by “baffling” bureaucracy, high fees and delays that leave many older Australians dying before receiving care. The inquiry, chaired by the Greens senator, has been extended for a year after receiving almost 300 submissions.
author: Guardian World

title: Wife of Japanese journalist Yuki Imai pleads for his release after Russia detains him
content:
The wife of Japanese journalist Yuki Imai has issued an emotional appeal for his release after he has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying. Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid‑October while preparing to return to Japan from a two‑year assignment at the newspaper’s bureau in Yuzhno‑Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island.

Imai is being held in Moscow on allegations that he conducted “espionage” while working for the newspaper in Russia’s far east. The wife’s plea highlights her distress and her request that the authorities reconsider his detention.
summary: Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid‑October in Moscow on suspicion of espionage while preparing to return to Japan from a two‑year assignment in Yuzhno‑Sakhalinsk, Sakhalin. His wife has issued an emotional appeal asking for his release after more than a month of detention.
author: Guardian World

title: China says it may take necessary measures after Trump proposes 20% tariff
content: Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’ Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash. Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
summary: China says it may take necessary measures after Trump proposes 20% tariff.
author: Guardian World

title: Bob Woodward's memoir 'Secrets' details his career and the craft of investigative reporting
content: The journalist who helped bring down Nixon on false starts, Watergate, and the art of cultivating a source ‘I have always disliked the term ‘investigative reporter’.” So writes Bob Woodward, one of the most celebrated reporters of our time – the man whose Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein undoubtedly changed the US presidency and journalism itself for ever. His longtime boss, the Washington Post editor Ben Bradlee, disliked the term too: “All reporting is investigative,” Bradlee would say. The term conjures a certain sophistication, perhaps, but part of the beauty of a reporter’s work is how deceptively unsophisticated it can be. Secrets is a far-ranging, revealing memoir of an extraordinary career, but more than that, it is an ode to grinding it out – knocking on doors, asking and asking again, listening, taking notes, making notes on the notes, patiently following every lead to exhaustion. In a media ecosystem saturated with fast and flimsy takes, this feels like a tonic. The real star of his story, Woodward seems to insist, is the shoe leather.
summary: Bob Woodward's memoir 'Secrets' is a far-ranging account of his extraordinary career, including his Watergate reporting with Carl Bernstein. The book emphasizes the deceptively unsophisticated nature of reporting, focusing on persistence and following leads.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Review: Jon Fosse's Vaim Hotel sequel explores surreal captivity in new novel
content:
Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel, Vaim Hotel, serves as the second volume in a loosely connected trilogy set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. The book is a sequel to Vaim and explores the experience of a man who is stripped of the elements that define his identity. Translated by Damion Searls, the narrative is written in Fosse’s characteristic hypnotically recursive style, consisting of a single sentence.

The story begins with a man in his 50s who drives to Vaim for reasons he cannot fully articulate. He decides to stay at the empty Vaim Hotel, unaware that he may never leave. The novel features Brita, the hotel owner, a mysterious female figure before whom the male protagonist’s agency fails. This dynamic mirrors the themes of the predecessor, where a man encounters a woman he secretly loved in his youth. In that earlier volume, the woman requests to move with him to their hometown on a boat named after her, despite being married.

The predecessor, Vaim, also depicts a man who has died, with the woman returning to her husband and demanding he answer to a specific name and move into the home of the man she had previously left him for. The husband describes these events as strange and chooses that word for his tombstone. Reviewers note that both books feature a sense of powerlessness in the men and a dream-like, surreal randomness to the events.

Fosse’s narrative choices in Vaim Hotel are described as thwarting easy rationalization. The work is characterized as Beckettian in its appreciation for the absurd and the tediously mundane. It is presented as a tale of captivity that is only slightly less disorienting than its predecessor, owing to the thematic connections between the two volumes.
summary: Jon Fosse's new novel Vaim Hotel is the second volume in a trilogy set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. The book features a man who lodges at the empty Vaim Hotel under the influence of its owner, Brita, in a story described as a tale of captivity.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Photographer Niall McDiarmid captures vibrant colors to counter muted world
content: Photographer Niall McDiarmid seeks out vivid colours, such as bright green kebab shops and red stockings, to counteract what he describes as a muted beige and monochrome world. The accompanying visual feature highlights these vibrant scenes as antidotes to everyday dullness.
summary: Photographer Niall McDiarmid seeks out bright colors, such as green kebab shops and red stockings, to provide an antidote to the world's muted beige and monochrome tones.

title: Andy Taylor, Duran Duran guitarist, dies at 65
content:
Andy Taylor, the guitarist for the 1980s pop band Duran Duran, has died at the age of 65.

He was diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, and publicly disclosed the diagnosis in 2022 as the band approached induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

Taylor’s career was marked by significant chart success during the 1980s.
summary: Andy Taylor, the guitarist for 1980s pop band Duran Duran, died at age 65. He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018 and publicly disclosed the diagnosis in 2022 as the band approached their Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction.

title: Strabane withdraws UK Town of Culture 2028 bid after causing division
content: The County Tyrone town was shortlisted as one of 15 possible locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with the chance to win £3m.
summary: Strabane, a town in County Tyrone, was shortlisted as one of 15 possible locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with a chance to win £3 million. The bid was later withdrawn after it caused great division.

title: Aaron Rodgers accuses Steelers coach Mike McCarthy of misconduct in ESPN interview
content: From a half-time huddle gone wrong to an ultimatum over play-calling, here’s what the quarterback said Wednesday in a scorched-earth appearance on Pat McAfee’s show Barely 12 hours after the Pittsburgh Steelers announced that Aaron Rodgers would be deactivated and Mason Rudolph would start Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos, the four-time NFL Most Valuable Player left no bridge unburned in a surprise call-in to ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show. In a 34-minute appearance on Wednesday afternoon where he spoke uninterrupted for long stretches, Rodgers accused Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in a quarterback meeting, skipping walkthroughs and falling behind on film study. He also said the 63-year-old McCarthy broke a half-time huddle against Philadelphia with the words “One, two, three, Packers”. According to Rodgers, McCarthy denied falling asleep at the team facility.
summary: Aaron Rodgers appeared on ESPN's The Pat McAfee Show to criticize Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy's preparation and play-calling. Rodgers alleged that McCarthy fell asleep in a meeting and used incorrect team names during a half-time huddle.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Alejandro Garnacho left out of Aston Villa plans despite Unai Emery's interest
content:
Unai Emery has reportedly left out Alejandro Garnacho from Aston Villa’s plans, a decision that mirrors the treatment of Harvey Elliott last season despite the club’s ongoing attacking struggles. This week marks three years since Garnacho scored for Manchester United in a 3-3 Champions League draw against Galatasaray in Istanbul. At that time, the winger was a teenage star and a regular starter, having recently won the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award for an overhead kick at Goodison Park.

During that period, Garnacho was central to Manchester United’s future, sharing the pitch with Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, who are now his teammates at Aston Villa. He continued to perform well, scoring twice in a 3-2 victory against Villa on Boxing Day and again in a win over West Ham, which led to a memorable celebration with Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund. Garnacho concluded that season by scoring against Manchester City at Wembley in the FA Cup final, cementing his status as a beacon of hope for the club alongside Mainoo.
summary: Unai Emery wanted the winger, but Alejandro Garnacho has been left out in the cold at Aston Villa despite the club's attacking struggles. The article notes this situation is similar to Harvey Elliott's experience at the club last season.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Gukesh and Sindarov draw Game 2 of world chess championship in 20 moves
content:
India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match on Wednesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs. The encounter concluded in just 20 moves and 1 hour 57 minutes, ending by threefold repetition. This result leaves the overall match score level at 1–all.

The game was notably brief, marking one of the shortest classical world title games since the reunification of rival championships in 2006. It was also the first game to finish in under two hours since Ding Liren and Ian Nepomniachtchi drew their 11th game in just over 100 minutes in Astana in 2023.

In this encounter, World champion Gukesh opened with the London System. The next game is scheduled for Thursday, with Sindarov set to play with the white pieces.
summary: India’s Gukesh Dommaraju and Uzbekistan’s Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their world chess championship match in 20 moves, leaving the score level at 1-all. Sindarov will play with white in Game 3 on Thursday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the Geneva suburbs.

content: Liverpool defeated Club Brugge in a clinical Champions League match, bouncing back from a previous defeat. Alexander Isak scored twice, with Florian Wirtz also finding the net to secure the victory for the hosts.
summary: Liverpool defeated Club Brugge in a clinical performance to bounce back from a previous Champions League defeat. Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz scored goals for the winning team.

content: Alexander Isak scored two goals against Club Brugge, increasing his season tally to ten. The striker continues to demonstrate the value of Liverpool’s £125m transfer fee from last year.

content: New data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) indicates that while annual inflation has increased, the country’s economic growth remains robust. The report presents these two contrasting trends in the current economic landscape.

content: U. S. Special envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “grandmaster of politics” following U. But he’s definitely a grandmaster of politics,” Kushner said…

title: Judge blocks Fulton County from handing 2020 ballot copies to state board
content: A Fulton County, Ga., judge on Wednesday paused her own order requiring the county to provide copies of ballots seized by the FBI earlier this year to the Georgia State Election Board. Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe suspended the directive, which she had issued Tuesday, after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.
summary: A Fulton County judge paused her order for the county to turn over seized 2020 ballot copies to the Georgia State Election Board. The judge acted after county election officials filed a notice of appeal regarding the order issued Tuesday.

title: Mayor Mamdani to miss postponed Macy's Thanksgiving parade due to Achilles surgery
content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) will miss the postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving parade on Saturday due to scheduled surgery on his right leg. The mayor confirmed at a Wednesday press conference that he is undergoing the procedure on Friday after tearing his Achilles tendon. Mamdani stated he was “very disappointed” to be unable to attend the rescheduled event.
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will miss the postponed Macy’s Thanksgiving parade because he is scheduled to have right‑leg Achilles tendon surgery on Friday. He confirmed at a Wednesday press conference that he could not attend the rescheduled event and expressed disappointment.

The judge dismissed the FCC’s lawsuit on jurisdictional grounds, prohibiting the agency from taking further action on ABC’s early license review.

title: Rod Simms argues Australia should tax gas industry to boost revenue
content:
Rod Simms argues that increasing tax revenue from Australia’s gas industry is a straightforward public policy measure. He notes that fossil fuel companies currently do not pay for the natural resources their businesses rely on. Simms contends that while there are calls for the government to return the budget to surplus, achieving this through large expenditure cuts is difficult due to rising costs associated with an ageing population and defence spending.

Simms suggests that successfully balancing the budget requires focusing on the revenue side alongside expenditure control. He identifies collecting more tax from the gas industry as the easiest step to address ongoing budget deficits, which are forecast to continue well into the future.
summary: Rod Simms states that fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resources their businesses depend on. He contends that collecting more tax from the gas industry is the easiest step to help address continuing budget deficits.

title: How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk
content: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. While research indicates that most firearm owners prioritize safety, current prevention strategies for youth have largely focused on policy change rather than teaching adolescents how to identify injury risk.
summary: Firearm injury is the leading cause of death for adolescents in the United States. Most firearm owners prioritize safety, research shows, but strategies aimed at firearm injury prevention among youth have largely focused on policy change instead of teaching them how to identify injury risk.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nearly half of Hungarian children exposed to screens by 18 months
content:
Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by the age of 18 months.  

What they need most for development, however, is play, physical activity, face‑to‑face interactions and active exploration of their surroundings.  

Early and intensive use of digital devices may pose risks not only because of the time spent in front of screens, but also because it can take time away from these essential experiences.
summary: Nearly half of Hungarian children are exposed to screens daily by 18 months. Early and intensive digital device use may take time away from play, physical activity, face‑to‑face interactions and exploration.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Culturally relevant nutrition interventions can engage Black adults more effectively
content: A recent study published in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior examined ways to better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions aimed at improving dietary habits and reducing cardiovascular risk.
summary: A recent study in the Journal of Nutrition Education and Behavior explored how researchers can better engage Black adults with hypertension in digital nutrition interventions. The interventions aim to improve dietary habits and reduce cardiovascular risk.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Ecuadorian Plant Piper carpunya Reduces Clostridium perfringens in Risotto
content:
A plant long used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador may help control bacteria in ready‑to‑eat foods.  
A study in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally called guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto model.
summary: A study in the journal Foods found that extracts of the Ecuadorian plant Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto model. The plant is traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later
content: A recent long‑COVID study found that 50 % of adults reported symptoms indicative of dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Participants with persistent breathing problems were generally younger, more often female, and had a lower likelihood of having been hospitalized during their acute COVID episode.
summary: Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue for lymphoma survivors
content: A recent study published online on November 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology reports that a multidisciplinary intervention can improve fatigue in lymphoma survivors who continue to experience persistent fatigue. The study found that the improvement in fatigue was sustained for up to six months after the intervention.
summary: A study published online Nov. 20 in the Journal of Clinical Oncology found that a multidisciplinary intervention improves fatigue in lymphoma survivors with persistent fatigue. The improvement was maintained for six months.
author: Medical Xpress

title: U.S. Age-Adjusted Stroke Death Rate Decreases 2000-2024
content:
Research published in the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report found that from 2000 to 2024 the age‑adjusted stroke death rate in the United States fell.  

However, the study noted that rates increased among certain groups during the most recent trend periods.
summary: During 2000 to 2024, there was a decrease in the age-adjusted stroke death rate, although rates increased among certain groups in the most recent trend periods, according to research published in the U. S.

title: Bank of England says UK food inflation may reach 5% next year
content:
The Bank of England has warned that food price inflation in the UK could reach 5 % next year.  The forecast is driven by mounting cost pressures, an energy price‑cap rise and a possible impact from El Niño, according to the bank’s latest assessment.

The bank noted that, although food inflation is expected to accelerate, it has risen less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.  This suggests that the current trajectory is more moderate than earlier projections.

Deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross‑party Treasury Select Committee that food price inflation is coming in under what the bank had expected and even under what the industry had anticipated.
summary: Bank of England says UK food inflation may reach 5% next year.

title: Petr Sulc's Team Develops Programmable DNA Building System for Nanorobots and 3D Electronics
content: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system. This innovation could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics, and next-generation nanotechnology.
summary: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

title: Neolithic Denmark: Fermented Milk Held Ritual Power in Tombs
content: Experimental archaeology has examined the substances fermented in Neolithic Scandinavian pottery that were deposited in tombs. The findings suggest that fermented dairy products held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.
summary: Experimental archaeology indicates that fermented dairy products were deposited in Neolithic Scandinavian tombs. This suggests these substances held symbolic significance in prehistoric funerary rituals.

title: Archaeologists find evidence of hunter‑gatherers in Ireland 13,500 years ago
content: A team of archaeologists and scientists has uncovered evidence suggesting Late Upper Paleolithic hunter-gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago. This discovery potentially pushes the confirmed timeline of human arrival in the region back by nearly a millennium.
summary: A team of archaeologists and scientists uncovered evidence that Late Upper Paleolithic hunter‑gatherers may have lived in southern Ireland around 13,500 years ago. This would place human presence in the region nearly a millennium earlier than currently confirmed.

title: Sweden tops global media freedom support rankings
content: A new index has ranked Sweden as the world’s leading supporter of international media freedom. The same study notes a decline in funding from 30 major donor countries, even as threats to independent journalism continue to rise.
summary: Sweden was ranked the world's leading supporter of international media freedom in a new index. The index also notes a decline in funding from 30 leading donor countries amid growing threats to independent journalism.

title: Study finds dislike of AI doesn't reduce its impact on decisions
content: New research from City St George’s, University of London shows that an aversion to artificial intelligence does not reduce its influence on people and their decision‑making. The study indicates that even those who dislike AI remain affected by the technology in their choices.
summary: New research from City St George's, University of London finds that an aversion to artificial intelligence does not lessen its influence on people. The study says AI continues to affect decision‑making even among those who dislike it.

title: Meat-Eating Dinosaurs Likely Sawed Meat with Backward-Dragging Teeth, Experiments Show
content: New experiments suggest that meat‑eating dinosaurs likely fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh, much like a saw, rather than biting straight down like a dagger. The study proposes that this tearing motion was a key feature of their feeding behavior.
summary: New experiments suggest that meat-eating dinosaurs fed by dragging their teeth backward through flesh like a saw. This contrasts with the idea that they bit straight down like a dagger.
author: Phys.org

title: Anthropic mathematician claims to solve generalized Riemann hypothesis with Claude
content:
Mathematics is facing an existential crisis.  

On November 20, 2026, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic claimed that while working with the model Claude, he had solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis, the most famous problem in mathematics.  

The hypothesis has remained unsolved for 167 years, and solving it could easily warrant a Fields Medal—considered equivalent to a Nobel Prize, but for mathematics.
summary: On Nov. 20, 2026, a mathematician at Anthropic claimed to have solved the generalized Riemann hypothesis while working with the model Claude. The problem had remained unsolved for 167 years and solving it could earn a Fields Medal, the mathematics equivalent of a Nobel Prize.
author: Phys.org

title: Questioning the Claim That We Know More About Space Than the Ocean
content: New discoveries about the world are made daily, from a species of deep‑sea fish to a new galaxy. A common saying claims we know more about space than the ocean, but this assertion is debated. The question hinges on how “knowing” is measured—whether by the quantity of direct observations or by the resolution of those observations.
summary: New discoveries are made daily about the world, including a species of deep‑sea fish and a new galaxy. The statement "We know more about space than the ocean" is questioned, and the criteria for determining knowledge—direct observation versus resolution—are discussed.

title: MIT and UCSB physicists find Einstein's particle motion theory incomplete for quarks
content: MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists have found that Einstein’s classic theory of particle motion does not fully account for behavior of particles moving near light speed. Their calculations show that heavy quarks traversing an ultra‑hot plasma receive rare, unusually powerful jolts that the traditional model cannot explain.
summary: MIT and UCSB physicists find Einstein's particle motion theory incomplete for quarks.

title: Astronomers discover Phoebe, a primordial black hole only three times the Moon's mass
content:
Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before first stars. Object named Phoebe was detected when it briefly magnified a distant star.  

Phoebe could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. Its estimated mass is only three times that of the Moon, and it may be a 13‑billion‑year‑old relic that offers new clues to dark matter.
summary: Astronomers detected Phoebe when it briefly magnified a distant star, suggesting it could be a primordial black hole formed after the Big Bang. The object has an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon and may be a 13‑billion‑year‑old relic that could provide clues to dark matter.

title: Researchers find drug boosts energy expenditure without activating brown fat
content: Researchers have found that a drug can markedly raise the body’s energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie‑burning brown fat. This unexpected result highlights a new obstacle in developing obesity treatments that rely on the body’s natural fat‑burning mechanisms.
summary: Researchers discovered a drug that significantly increases the body's energy expenditure. The finding presents a challenge for developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement shows no pain or mobility benefit
content:
A landmark clinical trial, the largest of its kind, evaluated robot‑assisted knee replacement surgery. The study highlighted the technology’s potential for greater surgical precision.  

Despite this advantage, the trial found that, after one year, patients showed no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional knee replacement surgery.
summary: The trial found no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery after one year compared with conventional surgery. Robot-assisted knee replacement offers greater surgical precision.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find brine‑pool lakes over a mile below Red Sea
content: Scientists have identified rare underwater lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea. The brine pools, described as extremely salty and oxygen‑free, are teeming with microbial life. Researchers say these environments may reveal secrets about Earth’s ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life, challenging current ideas of where organisms can survive.
summary: Scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea. The lakes, known as brine pools, are extremely salty, oxygen‑free and host microbial life, offering clues about ancient oceans and potential alien life.

title: Ask HN Feed Starved by Decline in Text Posts; Separate Ranking Proposed
content:
A Hacker News user has identified the cause behind the recent scarcity of posts on the /ask page, which had prompted community discussions about missing pagination and low post counts. The issue stems from the traditional method of selecting Ask HN stories, which were drawn from the top 1,500 ranked submissions used to generate the front page. According to the user, the proportion of text-based submissions within this top tier has declined significantly, effectively starving the Ask HN feed of new content.

To resolve this, the proposed solution is to calculate a separate list of ranked Ask HN posts rather than relying on the general front page ranking. The user clarified that while "Ask HN" is the conventional name for these entries, the category includes any post submitted without a linked URL, regardless of whether the title begins with "Tell HN" or another prefix. This post has received 87 points and 38 comments.
summary: The /ask page was running dry of Ask HN posts because the top 1500 ranked submissions list had a low percentage of text posts. The proposed solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs.
author: Hacker News

title: 1Password breach exposes customer names and emails, not passwords
content:
1Password reported that a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach did not expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but it could increase users’ risk of phishing attacks.

The company began investigating the incident on November 19 after an attacker accessed an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker retrieved 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. The number of affected users remains unknown.
summary: A hacker accessed 1Password's backend systems and stole customer names and email addresses, but did not obtain passwords or vault data. The breach began after an attacker compromised an employee's GitHub account and injected malicious code into backend services.
author: The Verge

title: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa
content:
EPA reports “zero” airborne lead following a controlled Army detonation in Iowa.  

On November 25, 2026, the U.S. Army detonated more than 9,700 pounds of highly‑volatile, degraded lead azide on the grounds of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. The detonation was carried out to prevent a possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps. Video footage showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.

After the blast, the Army confirmed that all barrels at the plant were destroyed and that no secondary explosions or infrastructure damage occurred. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it's absolutely humanly poss …” the Army spokesperson said.
summary: EPA reports ‘zero’ airborne lead following controlled Army detonation in Iowa.
author: The Verge

title: WhatsApp Adds Scheduled Messaging Feature for Private and Group Chats
content: WhatsApp's 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it's on WhatsApp too. If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don't want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too. Meta: To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It …
summary: WhatsApp now lets its 3 billion users schedule messages for private and group chats up to two weeks in advance. The feature, described by Meta as highly requested, works with text, photos, and videos and is accessed by holding the send button to set a date and time.
author: The Verge

title: Google’s My Channel patent seeks AI‑generated video feeds based on user data
content:
Google filed a patent last year for a system called My Channel that is designed to create feeds of personalized, AI‑generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent was rejected, but Google may appeal or resubmit an amended version, potentially bringing the concept to market.

The patent was first spotted by Patentlyze. It was filed last May and published last week. It describes using a person's demographic data and viewing history to create prompts that are fed into a large language model to generate AI videos tailored to that user.
summary: Google filed a patent for My Channel, a system that would create personalized AI‑generated video feeds and ads using users' demographic data and viewing history. The patent was rejected, but Google may appeal or resubmit, which could bring the system to market.
author: The Verge

title: Amazon ordered to recall over 400,000 hazardous products after court ruling
content:
Amazon has been ordered to recall more than 400,000 hazardous products after a court decision in its favor of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). The U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland ruled that Amazon is a distributor of goods, not merely a logistics provider, and therefore must carry out recalls of third‑party items.  

Amazon filed suit against the CPSC in March 2025 following the agency’s directive to recall over 400,000 “Fulfilled by Amazon” products that pose a substantial product hazard. The recalled items include faulty carbon monoxide detectors, hair dryers lacking electrocution protection, and child products.
summary: Amazon ordered to recall over 400,000 hazardous products after court ruling.
author: The Verge

title: Google Familiar Faces AI adds support for Walmart’s $35 Onn Outdoor Camera
content:
Google has added its Familiar Faces AI detection to two Walmart‑branded cameras. The $35 Onn Outdoor Camera Plug‑In and the $77 Onn Floodlight Camera Hardwired now support the feature through a Google Home update, though users must have a Google Home Premium subscription to enable it.  

Both Onn models, along with Google’s Nest Cam Outdoor (wired, 2nd gen), also receive a new remote control in the Google Home app that lets users start or stop a 30‑second security siren while viewing the live video feed. Earlier this month, Google announced Gemini Live.
summary: A Google Home update adds Familiar Faces support to Walmart’s $35 Onn Outdoor Camera Plug‑In and $77 Onn Floodlight Camera Hardwired. Access to the feature still requires a Google Home Premium subscription, and both cameras now include a remote control in the Google Home app to trigger a 30‑second security siren while viewing live video.
author: The Verge

title: Physicist Suvrat Raju tests AI on unpublished problem, plans benchmark
content:
A professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, Suvrat Raju, recently tested a frontier artificial‑intelligence model by giving it a physics problem he had already solved but not published. Because the problem had never appeared online, Raju intended to see whether the model could answer a question it could not have simply memorized.

The AI’s response was incorrect, yet it performed better than Raju had anticipated. The unexpected level of competence led him to consider repeating the experiment in a more formal way. Together with a colleague, Raju is now working to develop a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate AI systems on theoretical‑physics problems that have not been previously documented online.
summary: Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem he had already solved but not published. The model answered incorrectly but better than expected, prompting Raju and a colleague to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.
author: Ars Technica

title: Kagi launches privacy‑focused Gmail rival Kagi Mail with calendar
content:
Kagi, a small software company based in Palo Alto, California, has expanded its subscription‑based search engine offering by launching a Gmail‑like email service called Kagi Mail. The service is positioned with the same emphasis on privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization and user control that Kagi promotes for its search product. Alongside the email platform, Kagi is also introducing a calendar feature, both of which are currently available only through web interfaces.

The email interface, which is in public beta, is described as minimalist and keyboard‑command driven, providing a private, ad‑free experience. Kagi Mail includes unlimited aliases and domains, an anti‑lock‑in policy for user data, 50 GB of storage, rule‑based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional AI tools that are off by default—such as an agent for searching email history, large‑scale re‑labeling, and creating additional filtering rules. Native Android and iOS apps are slated for release in the fourth quarter of next year.
summary: Kagi, a Palo Alto subscription‑based search engine company, has introduced Kagi Mail, a Gmail‑like service that emphasizes privacy, data sovereignty and customization. The web‑only public beta provides 50 GB storage, unlimited aliases, a calendar, rule‑based filtering and optional AI features, with native Android and iOS apps planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
author: Ars Technica

title: European spacecraft observes chaotic aftermath of NASA's DART asteroid deflection
content:
A European spacecraft has reported a chaotic scene following NASA’s asteroid‑deflection experiment. The experiment, carried out by a small solar‑powered probe launched four years ago, involved the spacecraft deliberately colliding with asteroid Dimorphos to test how humanity might alter the path of a body on a collision course with Earth.

The probe, part of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission, struck Dimorphos in September 2022 at a speed of more than 13,700 mph (6.14 km s‑1), releasing roughly 10 billion joules of energy. The impact shortened Dimorphos’s 12‑hour orbit around its larger companion, Didymos, by about 33 minutes—about 25 times the most conservative expectation. The collision destroyed the spacecraft as planned; DART captured images while aiming, and telescopes along with a small CubeSat detected the impact flash.
summary: NASA's DART mission slammed a solar‑powered probe into asteroid Dimorphos in September 2022, releasing about 10 billion joules of energy and shortening its 12‑hour orbit around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes. The impact destroyed DART, and only distant telescopes and a brief CubeSat detection recorded the aftermath.
author: Ars Technica

title: FCC approves SpaceX plan for AI data centers in space
content: The Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s proposal to place artificial‑intelligence data centers in orbit. In doing so, the agency dismissed several objections raised by opponents—among them claims that the project could threaten scientific research—stating that those concerns lie beyond the FCC’s regulatory jurisdiction.
summary: The FCC approved SpaceX's proposal to locate AI data centers in space. The agency dismissed opponents' concerns, including potential threats to scientific research, saying they fell outside its regulatory authority.
author: TechCrunch

title: Best gaming headsets of 2026 tested for value and performance
content:
The article reviews 20 gaming headsets, testing them to determine which models offer the best value for 2026. It covers a range of options, including wired, wireless, noise‑cancelling, and budget‑friendly headphones designed to enhance PC and console gaming experiences.

The piece highlights the growing importance of audio quality in modern games. Many titles now support 3D or spatial audio, allowing players to pinpoint the source of sounds such as explosions, dialogue, or the breathing of nearby monsters. This capability is especially useful in survival‑horror games, where hearing a zombie in the next room can be crucial, and in shooters like Fortnite and Apex Legends, where locating enemy footsteps can determine the outcome of a match.

The article also briefly mentions the best gaming chairs, though it does not provide specific details about those models.
summary: The article tests 20 gaming headsets to identify which are worth the cost in 2026. It reviews wired, wireless, noise‑cancelling and budget models and highlights 3D or spatial audio features used in games such as Fortnite and Apex Legends.

title: Indonesia search continues for workers trapped after confectionery factory fire kills 26
content: The death toll from a fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has risen to 26. Rescue workers are still searching the rubble for workers who remain trapped after the blaze.
summary: A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta has killed 26 people. Rescue workers are still searching for victims trapped under the rubble.

title: Russia to build Kaliningrad rail ferries, due 2030, citing transport blockade
content: The ferries, due in 2030 and costing around 50 billion roubles, will run between Baltiysk and Ust-Luga and be built in occupied Crimea. Most freight to Kaliningrad has already moved to sea routes, since Lithuania and Poland restricted transit after the 2022 invasion.
summary: Russia plans to construct rail ferries between Baltiysk and Ust‑Luga in occupied Crimea, costing around 50 billion roubles and slated for completion in 2030. The move follows Lithuania and Poland’s restriction of overland transit after the 2022 invasion, which has shifted most Kaliningrad freight to sea routes.

title: Iran orders Hormuz closure day by day amid unconfirmed tanker mine claims
content: The IRGC claimed three tankers hit mines in the crucial strait while under US escort, which the Joint Maritime Information Centre said was unconfirmed, as Qatar's prime minister pressed Rubio and Vance to restart talks.

title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat, shuts Bern's new Pyongyang office
content: North Korea has expelled a Swiss diplomat and ordered the closure of the Swiss office in Pyongyang that Bern opened on 19 October. The office was inaugurated when Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis traveled to Pyongyang and met senior officials, including his counterpart Choe Son Hui.

title: Wrongly deported Salvadoran reaches Madrid after 20‑month US lawsuit
content: A Salvadoran who was mistakenly deported to a prison in El Salvador in 2025 has concluded 20 months of litigation in the United States. He arrived in Madrid, Spain, which his lawyers say is the first stop of a temporary stay abroad.
summary: The Salvadoran was mistakenly deported to a prison in El Salvador in 2025. After 20 months of litigation in the United States, he arrived in Madrid, which his lawyers say is a temporary stay abroad.
author: Euronews

title: US proposes tariffs on 14 economies, expert says Trump lashing out indiscriminately
content:
The United States announced on Wednesday a set of proposed tariffs targeting 14 economies, including the European Union and China, after a months‑long investigation into alleged excess production. The move follows a broader effort by the administration to address trade imbalances and industrial overcapacity.

In an interview with France 24’s Sharon Gaffney, Dean Baker, senior economist at the Centre for Economic and Policy Research, criticized the new tariffs. He said the U.S. should work with the EU and Canada to establish clear, mutually beneficial ground rules for China’s participation in the world trade system. Baker described President Trump’s approach as “lashing out really indiscriminately” and doubted its productivity.
summary: The United States unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including the European Union and China, after a months‑long probe into alleged excess production. Dean Baker, Senior Economist at the Centre for Economic and Policy Research, said President Trump is lashing out indiscriminately and that the approach is unlikely to be productive.
author: France 24

title: Israeli lawmakers move to establish October 7 inquiry despite Netanyahu opposition
content: Israel’s new parliament on Wednesday took its first step toward establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack. The proposal has long been opposed by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to FRANCE 24’s Selina Sykes.
summary: Israel's new parliament took a first step on Wednesday to set up a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack. The move has been long opposed by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
author: France 24

title: Roma draw 2-2 with PSG after Donyell Malen penalty, ending PSG's Champions League run
content: Donyell Malen converted a 78th‑minute penalty to give Roma a 2‑2 draw at Paris Saint‑Germain on Wednesday. The result ended PSG’s unbeaten run in this season’s Champions League and snapped a 12‑game winning streak across all competitions, leaving Real Madrid as the sole team still unbeaten after five league‑phase matches.
summary: Roma draw 2-2 with PSG after Donyell Malen penalty, ending PSG's Champions League run.
author: France 24

title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies at 65 after prostate cancer
content: Andy Taylor, the guitarist whose riffs helped define Duran Duran’s sound and drive the British band’s 1980s global success, has died at age 65. The band and his family announced his death on Wednesday, noting it followed a long battle with prostate cancer.
summary: Andy Taylor, guitarist for Duran Duran, died aged 65. The band and his family said he had been battling prostate cancer, announcing his death on Wednesday.
author: France 24

title: Storm forces historic postponement of New York's 100th Thanksgiving Parade to Saturday
content:
A powerful storm forecast to bring fierce winds and heavy rain to the northeastern United States has led officials to postpone New York City’s 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade. The event, originally slated for Thursday, will now take place on Saturday, marking an unprecedented delay in the parade’s history.

City officials warned that Thursday’s weather could bring down tree limbs and power lines, creating a safety risk for the parade’s giant balloons and the crowds gathered below. The decision to reschedule reflects concerns over those hazards.
summary: A powerful storm forecast to bring fierce winds and heavy rain forced the unprecedented postponement of New York City's 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, moving it to Saturday. Officials warned Thursday's conditions could knock down tree limbs and power lines, creating safety risks for the parade's balloons and crowds.
author: France 24

title: UN rights chief Volker Türk warns of growing risk of atrocity crimes against Palestinians
content: UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Wednesday that the risk of additional atrocity crimes by Israel against Palestinians is widening. He said recent violence in the occupied West Bank has heightened existential fears among Palestinians.
summary: UN human rights chief Volker Türk warned on Wednesday of a widening risk of further atrocity crimes by Israel against Palestinians. He said recent violence in the occupied West Bank has heightened existential fears.

title: Palestinian journalist Mariam Dagga posthumously wins Rory Peck prize
content:
Mariam Dagga, a Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza by an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists. The organisers announced the award on Wednesday.

Dagga shares the prize with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press—Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi—who were honoured “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.
summary: Mariam Dagga, a 33‑year‑old Palestinian war correspondent killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, was posthumously awarded the Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists. She shares the award with Associated Press colleagues Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi for their coverage of the war’s human cost.
author: Guardian World

title: UN tribunal says UNRWA sacked Palestinian staff on unproven Israeli claims
content:
A UN tribunal has ruled that the evidence used to justify the 2024 sacking of Palestinian aid workers was “almost entirely” based on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and that the dismissals harmed humanitarian operations in Gaza. The judgment, reported by the Guardian, calls into question the basis for the UN Relief and Works Agency’s (UNRWA) decision to terminate staff.

UNRWA’s action was taken on the grounds of Israeli allegations that the dismissed workers were involved in the Hamas‑led attacks on 7 October 2023. The tribunal’s ruling now raises fresh doubts about that decision and its impact on aid delivery in the Gaza Strip.
summary: A UN tribunal has doubted the evidence used to justify the 2024 dismissal of Palestinian UN aid workers, saying it was based almost entirely on unproven Israeli assertions. The tribunal said the UN Relief and Works Agency's decision damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.
author: Guardian World

title: Women killed by men in Ireland almost double in a year, study finds
content:
A study released Wednesday by the Irish charity Women’s Aid shows that the number of women killed by men in Ireland has almost doubled in the past year. The report notes 13 deaths so far this year, marking a sharp rise after a two‑decade decline that began to reverse in 2021.

Figures covering the past 30 years indicate that more than half of the victims were killed by a current or former partner. The data also reveal a broader surge in female homicide over the last five years, with the most pronounced increase occurring in the most recent 12‑month period.
summary: The study shows the number of women killed by men in Ireland has surged in the past five years and risen sharply in the past 12 months. After two decades of decline, deaths rose from 2021 and total 13 so far this year, according to a Women’s Aid report released on Wednesday.
author: Guardian World

title: EU-UK summit dominates London while EU veto collapses Cop31 climate pact
content:
Last week saw two contrasting diplomatic episodes involving the European Union. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU‑UK summit captured the attention of Westminster, yet the event “barely registered” in Brussels, according to the source. The summit’s prominence in London contrasted with its low profile on the continent.

A day later, the climate conference in Turkey – COP31 – collapsed after the EU, acting as a united bloc, vetoed a watered‑down climate pact. At the same time, the EU reportedly eased its own domestic green regulations. These paired incidents are presented as evidence of the EU’s current priorities, its capacity to wield collective power, and the areas where its influence may be limited.
summary: A tightly choreographed EU‑UK summit on Friday captured attention in London but received little notice in Brussels. On Sunday the EU forced a veto that collapsed the Cop31 climate deal, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home.
author: Guardian World

title: UK minister Andy Burnham says EU students will pay higher tuition fees than UK peers
content:
Andy Burnham has said that under the as‑yet‑finalised portion of the new UK‑EU agreement, EU nationals will be required to pay higher tuition fees than domestic UK students. He made the comment after being asked by Kemi Badenoch to rule out an equal fee rate for UK and EU students, to which the prime minister replied that such a proposal “will not be put on the table”.

Burnham described the fee issue as the principal element of the arrangement announced in Brussels on Friday. The specific terms have not been settled, and both parties have agreed to an additional six‑month period to reach a solution.
summary: Andy Burnham said EU nationals studying at British universities will have to pay higher tuition fees than their domestic UK counterparts. He added that the proposal for equal fees will not be put on the table after Kemi Badenoch’s request, and both sides have given an extra six months to reach a solution.

title: NASA deploys aircraft and satellite to monitor US Army's lead explosive detonation in Iowa
content:
NASA announced on November 24 that it has deployed three research aircraft and a satellite-based instrument to support the U.S. Army’s planned detonation of degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. The controlled detonation of five tons of aging explosives is scheduled for approximately 10 a.m. EDT on November 25. This timeline follows a one-week delay attributed to public concern regarding the potential release of lead and other toxic materials. The decision to proceed with the detonation was driven by fears that cooling winter temperatures or attempts to chemically neutralize the materials could result in an unexpected, uncontrolled explosion.

To facilitate the operation, NASA deployed a P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III from the Langley Research Center, and a B200 from NASA Ames. Additionally, the agency is utilizing its Tropospheric Emissions: Monitoring of Pollution (TEMPO) instrument, which is mounted on a commercial satellite orbiting Earth. NASA stated that it is working with federal partners to collect environmental and atmospheric data to inform the broader federal response. The use of TEMPO is considered particularly important because the materials being detonated include lead azide and other toxic components, which have raised significant local concerns about health repercussions.

In response to the potential release of toxic materials, officials are encouraging local residents to remain indoors with doors and windows closed for 24 to 28 hours following the detonation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has activated an emergency response to provide accurate public health communication and technical assistance. The CDC has also issued guidance for locals to mitigate exposure to toxic materials such as lead dust. A map provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers using satellite data highlights areas surrounding the plant where surface deposits of lead are expected to exceed maximum allowable amounts set by the Environmental Protection Agency. In this visualization, blue represents lead expected to exceed limits on windows, while green indicates floors.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that the agency was called upon to put its airborne and space-based sensors and scientific expertise to work in these challenging circumstances. While the event has generated concern both locally and nationwide, Isaacman addressed comparisons to the Chernobyl nuclear accident. He described it as "irresponsible" to characterize the event as a "Chernobyl event," noting that there is no reactor and no fission products involved. Isaacman emphasized that the operation is a controlled detonation of aging explosive material being handled responsibly.
summary: NASA is using three research aircraft and a satellite instrument to monitor the US Army's controlled detonation of five tons of aging explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that comparing the event to Chernobyl is irresponsible because it involves no nuclear reactor or fission products.
author: Space.com

title: Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali first foreign visitor to China's Tiangong
content:
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali became the first foreign astronaut to set foot inside China’s Tiangong space station.  He arrived aboard the Shenzhou‑24 spacecraft early on November 25, as announced by the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) in a Mandarin update that praised the station and welcomed partners from around the world.

Shenzhou‑24 lifted off from the Xichang launch site on Tuesday, November 24, at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT on November 25) aboard a Long March 2F rocket.  The crew consisted of commander Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and payload specialist Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan’s armed forces.  The three astronauts reached Tiangong a little over six hours later.  Tang and Wu will stay aboard for the usual six‑month stint, while Ali will return in about a week, riding home with two of the three Shenzhou‑23 crew members who arrived in May.

During his brief stay Ali will conduct a series of joint Chinese‑Pakistani experiments.  Four collaborative projects in biotechnology and materials are planned, and he will perform an in‑orbit experiment with photosynthetic cyanobacteria.  The third Shenzhou‑23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain on the station until Shenzhou‑24 returns, setting a Chinese record for the first astronaut from his country to live in low‑Earth orbit for a full year.

Shenzhou‑24 is the twelfth crewed mission to Tiangong, a three‑module, T‑shaped outpost that China finished assembling in late 2022.  The station is about 20 % the mass of the International Space Station, and China plans to expand it further.
summary: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former Pakistani armed forces pilot and payload specialist, arrived aboard Shenzhou-24 on Nov. 25, becoming the first international astronaut to enter China's Tiangong space station. He will stay for about a week to conduct joint Chinese‑Pakistani experiments, including an in‑orbit photosynthetic cyanobacteria study, before returning with two Shenzhou‑23 crew members.
author: Space.com

title: Cliff Booth sequel joins Hollywood's nostalgic wave contrasting old LA's glory
content: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).
summary: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a sequel to Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood that is set eight years later in 1977. The film is part of a recent wave of nostalgic works that contrast a past Hollywood heyday with its current state.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Jane Alexander recalls hate mail and casting couch rejection in 50-year career
content: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role.
summary: Jane Alexander discusses her 50 years of stardom, including receiving hate mail and death threats for her role in The Great White Hope. She also recounts rejecting the casting couch and having a beautiful encounter with Muhammad Ali.
author: Guardian Culture

title: GTA VI features real pianist Yuja Wang hosting in-game classical radio station
content:
Grand Theft Auto VI features a new radio station called Symphony FM, hosted by the real-life pianist Yuja Wang. The in-game character, referred to as DJ Yuja, curates a playlist of 16 classical music pieces for players. The article highlights how this musical selection influences gameplay, noting that listeners can engage with the station while driving or performing other activities within the game.

The writer describes an experience where listening to the finale of Tchaikovsky’s Fifth Symphony on the station led to a reckless driving incident. The intense energy of the music caused the player to crash into a G-Wagen on a one-way street in Vice City. The article also mentions other in-game scenarios, such as robbing a bank to Sibelius or mowing down an alligator to Mahler, illustrating the variety of classical music available on the 24 stations in the game.
summary: Grand Theft Auto VI includes a classical music radio station called Symphony FM, which is hosted by the real-life pianist Yuja Wang. Wang curated a playlist of 16 pieces for the game, allowing players to listen to classical music while driving.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Ava DuVernay's 14th Amendment documentary defends democracy against Trump
content: DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th, energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution, which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment, and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants. The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th specifically established birthright citizenship, due process and equal rights for all races under the law, and furthermore barred insurrectionists from holding public office, all of which Trump appears casually intent on vandalising, airily amnesiac about his oath to uphold the constitution.
summary: Ava DuVernay's 14th Amendment documentary defends democracy against Trump.

title: The Fox Review: Dario Russo's Peculiar Comedy Features Olivia Colman
content:
Dario Russo’s debut feature, The Fox, is described as a “messed-up fairytale” that blends elements of the Brothers Grimm with the style of Yorgos Lanthimos, all while carrying a distinctly Australian flair. The film features a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill, and Emily Browning. Russo, who is well-known for co-creating the spy comedy series Danger 5, brings a similar aesthetic to this project, characterized by a thick retro texture inspired by 1960s and 1970s men’s magazines.

Set in a universe where animals can speak to humans, the comedy is noted for being delightfully peculiar. The review highlights that the premise of talking animals is actually the least weird aspect of the film. The movie is praised for its unique vibe, feeling as though it was created in consultation with the animal world itself.
summary: Dario Russo's debut feature, The Fox, is described as a "messed-up fairytale" set in a universe where animals can speak to humans. The film features a cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill, and Emily Browning.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album review praises star-packed soundtrack
content:
The soundtrack for Grand Theft Auto VI has been released, offering a compilation of brand new material from major artists across pop, rap, rock, and country genres. The album features imaginative collaborations and guest appearances, allowing listeners to enjoy the music independently of the game’s violent crime narrative or lifestyle fantasy elements.

The opening track, “Starting from Zero,” is performed by the duo Justice, who also composed the game’s original score released on December 11. This song features Michael McDonald of the Doobie Brothers singing an 80s-style pop ballad that includes a saxophone outro. The musical style reflects the game’s setting, a fictionalized version of Florida previously depicted in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was known for its inclusion of 80s hits.

Other tracks on the album include contributions from Dua Lipa, Travis Scott, and various Latin talent. While the game itself may not appeal to all bystanders, the soundtrack is described as a zeitgeisty collection that remains at the cutting edge of current music trends.
summary: The Grand Theft Auto VI soundtrack features brand new material from major pop, rap, rock, and country artists, including Dua Lipa and Travis Scott. The album opens with a track by Justice that features Michael McDonald and incorporates 80s nostalgia to match the game's Florida setting.

title: Deandra Dottin out on unattended stumps under new WBBL timed-out rule
content:
Deandra Dottin of the Melbourne Renegades was dismissed in an unusual manner during a Women’s Big Bash League match against the Brisbane Heat on Wednesday. After failing to reach the crease in time, the all-rounder was out as Brisbane bowler Sarah Glenn struck her unattended stumps. Dottin stated that the incident was something she had never seen before.

The dismissal resulted from the competition’s new timed-out rule, which requires an incoming batter to be ready within 75 seconds of a previous dismissal. If the batter is not prepared, they must stand aside for the first ball of their innings, allowing the bowler an opportunity to strike the stumps.
summary: Deandra Dottin was dismissed when a delivery from Sarah Glenn struck her unattended stumps after she failed to reach the crease in time. The incident occurred under the Women’s Big Bash League’s new timed-out rule, which requires batters not ready within 75 seconds of a dismissal to stand aside for the first ball.

The bank’s most recent involvement in a significant football transaction was its role in FIFA’s unsuccessful attempt to sell 20% of its commercial rights last summer.
summary: Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund is looking to sell up to 25% of Newcastle United by issuing new shares. JP Morgan has been appointed to handle the sale, which seeks investment to fund infrastructure projects.

content:
Raheem Sterling avoided jail after pleading guilty to a prolonged period of reckless driving while impaired by nitrous oxide. He received a suspended 12‑month sentence, to be enforced over an 18‑month period, and must carry out community service.

The sentence was read by district judge Kirsty Allman at Basingstoke magistrates court. Sterling, a former England international who led the Three Lions to a European Championship final five years ago, stood expressionless in the dock as the judgment was delivered.
summary: Raheem Sterling received a 12‑month jail term suspended for 18 months after pleading guilty to reckless driving while impaired by nitrous oxide. District judge Kirsty Allman ordered him to complete community service at Basingstoke magistrates court.

content:
On the podcast Stateside with Kai and Carter, host Kai Wright interviews environmentalist and author Bill McKibben to discuss the current state of the climate emergency in the United States. title: World records six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels
content:
For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days with temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, according to The Guardian. Daily global surface temperatures reached a record 2.24C above baseline on Monday, and the hot streak is forecast to continue.

While this brief record does not signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, scientists described it as an early indication of future conditions unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. The event is also likely to contribute to growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.
summary: The world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels for the first time. Scientists noted that while this brief streak does not breach Paris Agreement targets, it indicates potential acceleration of global heating.

title: Record 8.11ft tides in La Jolla flood California roads and businesses
content:
Super El Niño weather triggered record-breaking high tides along the California coast on Wednesday, causing seawater to flood roads and businesses in beachside communities. La Jolla, located just north of San Diego, recorded an all-time high tide of 8.11 feet (2.5 meters), according to the National Weather Service (NWS). Preliminary data indicated that Monterey, south of San Francisco, may have also set an all-time record with tides reaching 8.03 feet, as reported by an NWS meteorologist and the station’s historical weather data.

Due to safety concerns, the city of Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public. These closures are scheduled to remain in effect until Friday.
summary: Super El Niño weather caused record-breaking high tides along the California coast, flooding roads and businesses in beachside communities. La Jolla set an all-time high tide record of 8.11 feet, while Monterey closed multiple beaches to the public due to safety concerns.

content:
A McGill‑led study examined HIV patients in Pune, India, who were treated with the WHO‑recommended tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir (TLD) regimen.

title: Rare sugar d-sorbose may aid control of allergic and autoimmune diseases
content:
Rare sugars are naturally occurring monosaccharides that are scarce in nature and are not readily used by the body as energy sources. Some of these sugars have physiological effects beyond sweetness, which has sparked interest in their potential health applications.

One such sugar, d‑sorbose, is a structural relative of d‑fructose. However, its effects on immune cells have remained unclear.

Regulatory T cells (Tregs), identified by the Foxp3 protein, help restrain excessive immune responses and maintain immune balance. Whether a rare sugar can promote these cells has been little explored.
summary: The rare sugar d‑sorbose, a structural relative of d‑fructose, has unclear effects on immune cells. Scientists are exploring whether it can promote Foxp3‑positive regulatory T cells that restrain excessive immune responses, which could help control allergic and autoimmune diseases.

content:
A new policy brief from the European OceanICU project warns that if marine organisms were unable to transport carbon into the deep ocean, atmospheric CO₂ levels could rise dramatically by 2100. title: Solar vortex and magnetic reconnection launch rotating jet, simulations show
content: Simulations have shown that a solar vortex combined with reconnecting magnetic fields can launch a rotating jet. Solar spicules—slender jets that lift relatively cool plasma from the lower solar atmosphere—are often observed to rotate as they evolve. Small‑scale vortices frequently appear between convection‑driven granules in the photosphere. Researchers still need to determine exactly how these photospheric vortices contribute to spicule formation and how much mass and energy the rising jets transport into the corona.
summary: Solar spicules are slender jets that lift cool plasma from the lower solar atmosphere, carry energy upward, and sometimes rotate. Small‑scale vortices between granules in the photosphere may help form spicules, but the mass and energy carried into the corona remain uncertain.

title: Lunar craters proposed as natural radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
content:
Engineers have long recognized that powering a future lunar base will be difficult because the Moon’s two‑week night can deplete batteries charged by solar panels during the two‑week day, and those batteries must also survive the extreme cold. For decades, plans have included using a nuclear reactor to provide at least part of the energy needed for a human settlement on the Moon.  

One proposal highlighted in the title suggests locating such reactors inside lunar craters, using the crater walls as natural, “free” radiation shields to protect the base and its occupants. This concept aims to address both the power‑generation challenge and the need for radiation protection.
summary: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge because the two‑week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels and the batteries must survive freezing temperatures. Engineers have planned to use nuclear reactors, and the proposal suggests using lunar craters as free radiation shields for those reactors.
