title: New Scientist Book Club praises Dark Eden's worldbuilding, notes controversial incest
content: The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013. Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too! Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.” Advertisement Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here. In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image. “I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.” The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers. “Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.” Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”. Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex. “Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”. But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel ).
summary: The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November, praising its imaginative worldbuilding and language. Members noted mixed reactions to the protagonist John Redlantern and the book’s casual incest.
author: New Scientist

title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
content:
The Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has challenged mathematicians since the 19th century, may have been solved through the use of artificial intelligence. While the consensus among mathematicians is that the AI-assisted proof is valid, experts note that it will require significant additional work to make the solution comprehensible to humans. This development is described as a watershed moment that highlights the limited understanding of AI’s capabilities. The article references a possibly apocryphal story about mathematician G. H. Hardy, who once joked about solving the hypothesis to prevent his ship from sinking, suggesting that Hardy would be astonished by the current state of affairs.

Leading mathematician Terence Tao had speculated as recently as last month that AI might eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but he predicted it might not occur before 2050. In contrast, some mathematicians are now considering whether their most difficult remaining problems could be resolved within months. This rapid progress is part of a year that has left the mathematical community reeling, with the potential solution to the Riemann hypothesis viewed as a decisive blow.

For non-mathematicians, the significance of this breakthrough is harder to interpret. The article notes that AI has seen incredible advances in mathematics and coding over the past year. These fields allow for rapid improvement because answers can be swiftly checked and iterated upon using computer code. In contrast, other human endeavors, such as art and zoology, involve the messy physical world or unknowable human taste, making verification far more difficult. Whether this verification gap can be closed is identified as a potentially major question for the current era.

author: New Scientist

title: Scientists send gravity‑encoded message through brick wall
content: Scientists have demonstrated a way to transmit a message through a brick wall using only gravity, an old elevator, and a highly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, the researchers encoded the word “Gravity” into minute changes in gravitational pull. Because gravity can pass through ordinary barriers, the signal was received on the other side of the wall. The experiment suggests a potentially revolutionary method of communication that bypasses conventional obstacles.
summary: Scientists transmitted the word "Gravity" through a brick wall by moving a massive counterweight between two positions, creating tiny changes in gravitational pull. The transmission used only gravity, an old elevator, and a sensitive detector, demonstrating that gravity can pass through ordinary barriers and may enable new communication methods.
author: Science Daily

title: Common Gut Antibody May Prevent Colon Cancer, Study Finds
content: Scientists discovered a hidden gut defense: a common antibody that may protect against colon cancer. In experiments, mice lacking the antibody developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the heightened risk, pointing to a potential new strategy for cancer prevention.
summary: Researchers found that mice lacking a common gut antibody developed more than twice as many colon tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, suggesting a new preventive strategy.
author: Science Daily

title: Peppermint oil lowers systolic blood pressure by 8.5 mmHg in 20 days
content:
A randomized study of 40 adults found that taking small doses of peppermint oil twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Participants who received a placebo showed no significant improvement in blood pressure.

The results suggest that peppermint oil could be a low‑cost, natural option for managing mildly elevated blood pressure.
summary: A randomized study of 40 adults found that taking small doses of peppermint oil twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Participants receiving a placebo showed no significant improvement, suggesting peppermint oil as a low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.
author: Science Daily

title: New Theory Proposes Chemical Encoding of Memory, Questioning AI Consciousness
content: A new theory proposes that the brain may encode and retrieve memories through chemical interactions rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers suggest that the interplay between brain cells and their molecular environment could explain the close link between memory, emotion, and thought. These findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human‑like consciousness.
summary: Researchers suggest the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories instead of relying only on electrical signals. The theory challenges the idea that powerful computers could develop human‑like consciousness.
author: Science Daily

title: Stanford scientists find three hidden brain types linked to ADHD and anxiety
content:
Stanford scientists used AI to analyze thousands of children’s brain scans and found three distinct brain types linked to ADHD and anxiety that do not align with traditional diagnoses.  

The patterns can appear before a diagnosis, which may allow earlier detection and more effective personalized treatments.
summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not fit traditional diagnoses. The hidden patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective personalized treatments.
author: Science Daily

title: Physicists trap and cool positron to near absolute zero in wall‑free trap
content:
Physicists have trapped a positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron, and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. The positron is suspended in a wall‑free trap, keeping it safely separated from ordinary matter.

The team plans to perform the most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any detected difference between the electron and positron could reveal cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.
summary: Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero in a wall‑free trap. The team will conduct the most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter, and any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model.
author: Science Daily

title: ESA's Euclid telescope discovers first unknown comet
content: ESA’s Euclid space telescope, built by the European Space Agency to investigate distant galaxies and the dark Universe, has detected its first previously unknown comet. The icy body lies about 1.3 billion kilometres from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.
summary: ESA’s Euclid space telescope, designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe, discovered its first previously unknown comet. The comet is about 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and has an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.
author: Science Daily

title: One in Three Older Adults with Dementia Take Harmful Meds, Study Finds
content: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes medications that can worsen brain function and raise the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Researchers note that, despite progress in the past decade, medication‑related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.
summary: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders take potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging despite progress over the past decade.
author: Science Daily

title: Beaver supermoon illuminates skylines worldwide in video
content: A video shows a striking supermoon rising above city skylines across the globe. The footage captures the November full moon appearing larger because it coincides with the moon’s nearest approach to Earth, a phenomenon known as a supermoon. This particular full moon is also called the “beaver moon,” a name that is believed to originate from the autumn practice of hunters setting traps for beavers to obtain warm fur for the winter.
summary: A supermoon rose over skylines around the world, as shown in a video. The November full moon, called the beaver moon, appears larger because it coincides with the moon’s closest approach to Earth, a name linked to hunters trapping beavers for winter fur.
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA Sees Eye of Sahara from ISS on Nov. 14, 2026
content:
NASA astronaut Luke Delaney captured an image of the Richat Structure, commonly called the “Eye of the Sahara,” from the International Space Station on November 14, 2026. Located in Mauritania, this geological dome is approximately 100 million years old and formed by igneous activity and uplift. The structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and consists of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

In this type of geologic formation, the rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than those forming the outer rings. The photograph provides a clear view of the eroded dome as the station orbited above the region.
summary: The Richat Structure, also known as the Eye of the Sahara, was observed from the International Space Station on Nov. 14, 2026. The 45‑kilometer‑wide dome in Mauritania is about 100 million years old and formed by igneous activity and uplift, containing both igneous and sedimentary rocks.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Studies Strawberries, Cucumbers, Lemon Basil for Future Space Menus
content:
As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are evaluating specific crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and menu variety far from Earth. Recent testing has identified strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential options for future explorers. These space crops offer functional benefits beyond sustenance, as they can absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water, capabilities that become increasingly critical as crewed missions extend farther from Earth.

Strawberries are among the few sweet fruits under consideration for spaceflight, valued for being nutritious, aromatic, and self-pollinating. Researchers at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida are growing strawberries in flight-like growth chambers to evaluate their potential. In a collaboration with The Australian Research Council Centre for Excellence in Plants for Space, the University of Melbourne, and the University of Western Australia, scientists recently tested a wild strawberry against NASA’s leading candidate, ‘Delizz.’ A study published in September in the journal Life Sciences in Space Research found that while Delizz produced large, red fruit, the wild strawberry yielded small, yellow fruit due to a recessive genetic mutation. Although the wild strawberry produced twice as many buds, flowers, and fruit as Delizz, it was not selected as the top candidate because it grew too many runners, which would occupy valuable space aboard a spacecraft.

Cucumbers represent a new category for space agriculture, as no crops from the gourd family have previously been grown in space. NASA-funded researchers recently evaluated cucumbers for growth, yield, and nutrition under spaceflight conditions. According to a study published in August in the journal HortScience, the plants showed some signs of enlarged leaves but produced a steady stream of edible fruit. Introducing such crop variety is intended to benefit astronauts’ diets and mental well-being while increasing plant biodiversity, which may improve the likelihood of crop success on long-duration missions.

Lemon basil, an edible herb with a citrus scent and taste, is also advancing in testing at NASA Kennedy. Researchers report that lemon basil has passed preliminary space crop testing and successfully underwent seed sanitization, a process required to remove microorganisms from seeds before spaceflight. The next steps for this crop include assessing its growth in plant pillows, which are designed to house plants aboard the space station. Fresh herbs like lemon basil are viewed as a solution to menu fatigue, helping to transform packaged meals into more satisfying options that support human health and performance in space.

In parallel with Earth-based research, capabilities are expanding in orbit. A new investigation from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division is set to launch to the International Space Station. This mission will deploy a first-of-its-kind prototype growth chamber intended to provide critical insights for developing crop production systems. These systems aim to support the cultivation of crops like those currently being tested for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions.
summary: NASA is researching strawberries, cucumbers, and lemon basil as potential space crops for future Moon and Mars missions, growing them in controlled chambers at Kennedy Space Center and the ISS. The Biological and Physical Sciences Division aims to develop systems that can absorb CO₂, produce oxygen, and recycle water to support long‑duration crewed missions.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Enhances Program with Mentor‑Protégé Agreement Between Boeing and GRACE Aerospace
content:
NASA’s Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP) hosted a ceremonial signing of a Mentor-Protégé Agreement between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace on October 29, 2026, at the U.S. Space and Rocket Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The event marked the announcement of the agency’s latest agreement under its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. The ceremony included representatives from both companies and NASA, with Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace; Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager for The Boeing Company; and Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator of the OSBP, pictured in the front row.

NASA stated that it is evolving how it works with small businesses to strengthen the domestic aerospace industrial base for future exploration missions. As part of this initiative, the agency is streamlining the application process for the Small Business Supplier Development Program. NASA is also reducing administrative requirements, accelerating review and approval timelines, and enhancing incentives for prime contractor participation. These changes are designed to make supplier development more accessible, efficient, and aligned with the agency’s mission needs.

Dwight Deneal, assistant administrator of the Office of Small Business Programs at NASA Headquarters in Washington, described the program as a mission-focused tool for strengthening industrial base readiness and mission success. He noted that simplifying participation and focusing developmental assistance on capabilities NASA needs most aims to build a stronger, more resilient supplier base capable of supporting the agency’s highest-priority missions.

Under the new agreement, The Boeing Company will provide structured assistance to help GRACE Aerospace expand its capabilities as a supplier of mission-critical aerospace hardware. Boeing will fund the agreement, which is valued at nearly $500,000. Christian Diamond, Mentor-Protégé Program manager and small business liaison officer for Boeing, said the company is proud to continue its relationship with NASA and looks forward to sharing its expertise to support the growth and long-term success of the small business while strengthening the supplier base.

GRACE Aerospace, which has two decades of experience supporting defense and aerospace customers, plans to use the partnership to prepare for increasingly complex aerospace and spaceflight programs. Pauline Sevigny, president and owner of GRACE Aerospace, expressed gratitude for participating in the program. She stated that the company looks forward to growing and learning from industry experts while supporting the mission of resilience and space superiority. The enhanced supplier program remains part of NASA’s broader Office of Small Business Programs.
summary: NASA’s Office of Small Business Programs (OSBP) hosted a ceremonial Mentor-Protégé Agreement signing between The Boeing Company and GRACE Aerospace on Oct. 29, 2026, at the U.

content:
A storm with strong winds and heavy rain is approaching New York, threatening the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.  

Officials warn that the weather could impact celebrations across the USA, with the parade at risk.

title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk welcomes baby girl while on ISS
content: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, on his first mission aboard the International Space Station, welcomed a baby girl. The birth occurred while he was in orbit, making him the fourth astronaut in history to miss the delivery of a child while serving on the ISS.
summary: Joshua Kutryk, a Canadian astronaut on his first space mission, welcomed a baby girl while aboard the International Space Station. He is the fourth astronaut in history to miss the birth of a child while on the station.

title: AI Overwhelms Open Records Systems While Fires Accelerate Permafrost Thaw
content:
The Download is a weekday newsletter that delivers a daily snapshot of what is happening in the technology world. Each edition pulls together a mix of short news briefs, in‑depth features, and links to podcasts that explore emerging trends.

In this week’s edition the focus is on how artificial intelligence is testing the limits of America’s right‑to‑know. The newsletter explains that AI is straining the country’s open‑records systems. Venture‑backed startups have raised more than $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and transform it into AI‑powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests, which creates confusion for agencies that must decide whether they are dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline. Some states are responding by passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, a move that could reduce public transparency.

The second feature is a narrated podcast from MIT Technology Review that follows researchers into a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus. The podcast recounts a July 2021 wildfire that stripped away the moss and soil that insulated the permafrost below. Five years later, scientists investigated how fighting fires could help keep the carbon locked in the ground. Their research revealed that as climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, permafrost thaw accelerates and releases greenhouse gases, and researchers are now working to break that cycle.

The newsletter also includes a curated list of ten other stories, ranging from AI‑related security breaches to advances in medical research, each with a brief headline and source. Readers are directed to the full articles on the respective outlets for more detail.

Overall, The Download’s current edition highlights the dual pressures of AI on public‑records transparency and the growing threat of Arctic fires to global carbon stores, while offering readers a snapshot of additional tech news from around the world.
summary: AI is straining America’s open records systems as investors raise upwards of $100 million to collect data from agencies and chatbots make it easier for individuals to file requests. A wildfire on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus has accelerated permafrost thaw, prompting researchers to investigate how firefighting could keep carbon locked in the ground.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: US data center expansion drives surge in natural‑gas power projects
content:
The rapid expansion of data centers in the United States is fueling a significant resurgence in natural gas usage, a trend that has accelerated since May 2025. While renewable energy sources like wind and solar, supported by batteries, technically offer alternatives to meet rising electricity demand, the current reality in the US is dominated by natural gas. This shift is exemplified by the Meta data center project in Louisiana, where plans have expanded significantly. The local utility increased its planned natural-gas plants from three to ten to accommodate the growing power needs of the facility.

Interconnection queues, which list power plants requesting connection to the grid, reveal a notable shift in energy planning. Historically dominated by renewable projects, these queues are now seeing a major uptick in natural-gas proposals, particularly within PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator. Covering parts of 13 states from Illinois to Washington, DC, PJM announced in August that it had accepted proposals for 715 projects with a total capacity exceeding 200 gigawatts. Nearly half of this total capacity represents natural-gas plants. According to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue, if all queued projects were built, the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid would rise from 61% to 67%.

This trend reflects a broader national pattern where natural gas has become the default source for meeting exploding power demand, as it is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country. The AI-driven rush is also impacting corporate environmental metrics. Meta’s 2026 Sustainability Report indicates that its emissions increased by 45% over the previous year, surpassing the increases reported by other hyperscalers: Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The report states that Meta is “reevaluating” its 2030 net-zero emissions goal, though specific details regarding the timeline or method for this decision are not provided.

In response to grid limitations, data center developers are increasingly planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. Meta’s report notes that when the grid cannot deliver power on the necessary timeline, the company will utilize other methods, including on-site power generation. This approach allows developers to bypass long wait times for grid interconnection. While large industrial facilities like chemical plants and mining operations have historically used on-site power, the scale of this new data center initiative is substantial. Over 100 such off-grid facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts, which is more than double the entire peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these sites were proposed since the beginning of 2025.

Despite the availability of alternative solutions such as pairing wind and solar with batteries or implementing demand flexibility measures, the evidence indicates a strong correlation between the AI boom and the natural-gas boom in the United States. The combination of expanded grid connections and new off-grid infrastructure underscores the central role of natural gas in powering the current data center expansion.
summary: In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: True Crime Community Drives Rising Violent Attacks via TikTok and AI
content: Research shared with WIRED indicates that attacks tied to a network of young people obsessed with mass shooters are rising sharply. The group, described as nihilistic, disseminates its message through TikTok and artificial‑intelligence tools, linking the “true crime community” to an increase in violent incidents.
summary: Research shared with WIRED shows attacks linked to a network of young people obsessed with mass shooters are greatly increasing. The nihilistic group uses TikTok and AI to spread its message.
author: Wired

title: Xteink’s pocketable X4 Classic e-reader is down to just $55 for Black Friday
content: Unsurprisingly, we’re already seeing some solid Black Friday deals on a wide variety of e-readers. Everything from the Kobo Libra Colour to last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is on sale, but if you’re looking for something much cheaper — or considerably smaller — the Xteink X4 Classic is in a league of its own. Thankfully, the tiny e-reader is down to a new low of $54.87 ($55 off) at Amazon, making it an especially affordable alternative to Amazon’s latest Kindle. Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader Where to Buy: $109 $54.87 at Amazon (black) $109 $54.87 at Amazon (white) $109 $59 at Xteink The X4 Classic is an updated version of Xteink’s original pocket-sized e-reader, one that features a miniature 4.3-inch E Ink display that makes it more pocketable than any current Kindle or Kobo model. Like the pricier X4 Pro — which also happens to be on sale direct from Xteink for $84 — it features both physical page-turning buttons and magnets that let you attach it to compatible smartphones. At just 2.4 ounces and 4.9mm thick, it’s also easy to slip into a pocket, while its larger 920mAh battery can last up to 10 days on a single charge. That said, unlike the X4 Pro, the Classic lacks a touchscreen and built-in reading light, meaning you’ll need an external light to read in the dark. However, like the Pro, it does support the excellent CrossPoint Reader software, which you can install yourself to improve the reading experience. You can even use it to read books borrowed through Libby or purchased from stores like Kobo, though it takes a few extra steps to do so. Still, if you want an inexpensive, distraction-free way to read on the go, the X4 Classic is hard to beat for less than half the price of a Kindle. Read our hands-on impressions of the Xteink X4.
summary: Unsurprisingly, we’re already seeing some solid Black Friday deals on a wide variety of e-readers. Everything from the Kobo Libra Colour to last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is on sale, but if you’re looking for something much cheaper — or considerably smaller — the Xteink X4 Classic is in a league of its own.

title: Amazon in talks to lift block on Meta's Muse AI shopping agent
content:
Amazon has reportedly entered discussions with Meta about allowing the company’s Muse AI agent to shop on its online marketplace, according to a Fortune report. The talks aim to lift Amazon’s current block on Muse, with the focus on the types of products the AI would recommend and how such activity could affect the retailer’s advertising revenue.

Amazon’s concerns center on the possibility of losing advertising income, as the company relies on human shoppers to view ads across its platform. The company is also wary of the quality of product search results that Muse would deliver to users, and whether the AI’s age‑verification capabilities meet its standards. The outcome of these negotiations remains uncertain.
summary: Amazon has held discussions about allowing Meta's Muse AI agent to shop on its marketplace, which could end the current block. The company says it is concerned about potential advertising revenue loss and the quality of product search results Muse would provide.
author: The Verge

title: Nothing previews AI Ear Note earbuds with call recording and case transcription features
content:
Nothing has provided a detailed preview of its upcoming Ear Note AI earbuds, which are scheduled for release on December 8th. The device features a charging case equipped with a microphone that can record, transcribe, and summarize conversations. Similar to the Ear 3, the case includes a "Talk" button for recording the user’s voice, alongside a new "Record" button designed to capture and transcribe conversations.

In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei explained that the Record button enables the earbuds to record calls and the case to record meetings. He described this functionality as a "first step toward a hardware context layer for AI."
summary: Nothing gave a detailed look at its upcoming Ear Note AI earbuds, scheduled for release on December 8. The earbuds can record calls, and the case’s Talk and Record buttons can record, transcribe and summarize conversations, according to CEO Carl Pei.
author: The Verge
