title: Man and Dog Escaped King Tide on Oregon Beach, Video Released
content:
Cannon Beach police posted a video showing a man walking his dog on the beach on Tuesday when a sudden surge of tide swept both of them toward the water. The footage captured the man narrowly escaping the current, and authorities reported that both he and his dog made it back to dry land without injury.

The police department noted that the man had previously received a citation for driving on another beach and had been warned to stay away from the ocean because a “king tide” was expected that day. The warning came after the tide’s unusually high rise threatened to engulf the shoreline.

“King tides” is not a scientific term; they are exceptionally high tides that typically occur during a new or full moon when the moon is at its perigee. The department’s statement added that rising sea levels, combined with El Niño and king tides, are putting the U.S. west coast at high risk of record flooding. The report cited California’s recent stress tests of low‑lying areas in San Francisco and the broader threat of high tides and floods expected over Thanksgiving.
summary: Cannon Beach police posted footage of a man and his dog being swept by a king tide on a beach, but both returned to dry land uninjured. The man had earlier been cited for driving on another beach and was warned to stay away from the ocean as a king tide was expected.
author: Guardian Environment

title: George Monbiot: No sustainable way to eat fish, slams Marine Conservation Society guide
content:
George Monbiot argues that fishing is as harmful to marine ecosystems as tobacco is to human health. He dismisses claims from conservation charities that certain fish are safe to eat, stating that those recommendations do little to protect marine wildlife. Monbiot calls the idea of a single “sustainable” fish choice a myth.

In April, the Marine Conservation Society released its Good Fish Guide, urging consumers to stop eating cod and instead choose hake. The guide presented hake as a more environmentally friendly option. Monbiot notes that the Society later acknowledged that hake had become overexploited due to increased fishing pressure.

Six months after the initial recommendation, the Society downgraded hake’s sustainability rating. The change was attributed to the species’ overexploitation. Monbiot questions how such a shift occurred, implying a lack of consistent or reliable guidance from conservation groups.
summary: George Monbiot argues there is no sustainable way to eat fish and criticizes advice from conservation charities. He points out that the Marine Conservation Society’s Good Fish Guide first urged eating hake instead of cod, then six months later downgraded hake as overexploited.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant to Detonate Lead Azide Stockpile Amid Public Concern
content:
The US Army plans to detonate the nation’s entire stockpile of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning. This controlled blast, scheduled for the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, follows multiple delays and an outpouring of public concern regarding potential health and environmental impacts. The facility is located in a small town in south-eastern Iowa with a population of approximately 400.

The operation aims to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the bomb-making chemical. Authorities warn that the explosion risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals within a 100-mile (160km) radius. The specific location where these toxins may land remains uncertain as it shifts according to changing weather forecasts.
summary: The US Army will detonate the entire 9,700‑lb stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning, after multiple delays. The controlled blast could release toxic chemical plumes within a 100‑mile radius, sparking public concern about health and environmental effects.
author: Guardian Environment

title: HIV Viral Control Needed, but Not Enough for Healthy Aging
content: A recent report notes that individuals with HIV display accelerated biological aging. Blood‑based biomarkers reveal functions resembling older individuals rather than peers of the same chronological age. The findings underscore that controlling viral replication is necessary but alone does not ensure healthy aging.
summary: HIV viral control is necessary but not sufficient for healthy aging. Individuals with HIV exhibit signs of faster biological aging than people without HIV, with blood biomarkers resembling those of older individuals.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Methylmercury impairs forebrain inhibitory circuits and causes abnormal behavior in mice
content:
Global efforts to curb mercury pollution have not eliminated the threat posed by methylmercury (MeHg). The compound continues to persist in the environment, bioaccumulating along aquatic food chains. Humans mainly encounter MeHg through contaminated seafood. The devastating neurological effects of MeHg poisoning were first highlighted by Minamata disease, officially recognized in Japan in 1956. 

Since that time, researchers have examined MeHg’s neurotoxic impact, noting sensory, motor, and psychiatric symptoms. Although clinical reports document behavioral disturbances in affected individuals, the specific neural circuits responsible for these abnormalities remain poorly understood.
summary: Methylmercury impairs forebrain inhibitory circuits and induces abnormal behavior in mice. Clinical reports show behavioral disturbances in people exposed to MeHg, but the neural circuits responsible remain poorly understood.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Doctor reflects on US losing measles elimination status
content: A doctor reflects on the United States losing measles elimination status, noting that for many physicians of his generation, measles was rarely—or never—saw in practice. That was a sign of how well vaccination and public health efforts had worked.
summary: The doctor says many physicians of his generation rarely saw measles in practice. He says this rarity indicated successful vaccination and public health efforts.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FDA approves first new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer in over 20 years
content: The FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early‑stage breast cancer, the first such approval in more than two decades. This marks a significant shift in treatment for the most common form of the disease.
summary: The FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer. This is the first such approval in more than two decades.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Long‑term rise in fasting blood sugar linked to poorer midlife cognition
content: New independent research published in the Journal of the American Heart Association finds that young adults with progressive rises in fasting blood sugar over multiple decades were more likely to have worse cognitive health by midlife. Participants who developed type 2 diabetes during the study also showed signs of structural brain changes.
summary: Young adults who experienced a progressive rise in fasting blood sugar over multiple decades were more likely to have worse cognitive health by midlife. The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, also found that participants who developed type 2 diabetes had signs of structural brain changes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Single Vaping Episode Impairs Vascular Function, Study Finds
content: Researchers find a single vaping episode impairs vascular function, even when vaping without nicotine. The study’s results will be presented next week at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America.
summary: Researchers found that a single vaping episode can negatively affect vascular function, even without nicotine. The study results will be presented next week at the RSNA annual meeting.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Feng Jian's team discovers cytokinin–NIN module driving spontaneous root nodules in alfalfa
content: A research team led by Professor Feng Jian of the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) at the Chinese Academy of Sciences has identified a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module linked to spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa). This discovery explains how alfalfa can form nodules without rhizobia.
summary: Professor Feng Jian's research team at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module linked to spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa. The discovery shows how alfalfa can form root nodules without rhizobia.
author: Phys.org

title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
content:
Ultrathin “rainbow” sails have been proposed as a way to power spacecraft and shade the Earth. The idea builds on the physics of solar sailing, a concept that uses the momentum carried by photons in sunlight to generate a gentle push when the light bounces off a surface.

Solar sailing has gained renewed attention over the past decade, with several proof‑of‑concept flights demonstrating that the force from photons is sufficient to propel a spacecraft. These demonstrations confirm that the technology is feasible and could enable new forms of propulsion and planetary protection.
summary: Solar sailing uses the momentum of photons to push on surfaces, enabling propulsion. Proof‑of‑concept flights in the last decade have shown that solar sailing is indeed feasible.
author: Phys.org

title: 2026 Hurricane Season: El Niño Drives Record Pacific Storms, Calms Atlantic
content:
The 2026 hurricane season, ending Nov. 30, will be noted for stark contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic sign of a very strong El Niño.

Atlantic activity was below normal, while Pacific activity was above average, including two disasters in Hawaii.
summary: The 2026 hurricane season, ending on Nov. 30, saw below‑normal activity across the Atlantic basin and above‑average activity in the Pacific, a classic sign of a very strong El Niño. The Pacific experienced two disasters in Hawaii.
author: Phys.org

title: What draws data centers to a community?
content:
Oklahoma communities are currently evaluating proposals for new data center projects.  

Research co‑authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor provides insight into the factors that attract major technology companies to specific locations and explains why those decisions have local significance.
summary: As Oklahoma communities weigh new data center development, research co-authored by a University of Oklahoma architecture professor offers insight into what draws major technology companies to locations—and why those choices matter locally.
author: Phys.org

title: Star Obliquity Likely Has Little Impact on Planet Habitability
content: The article explains that a star’s axial tilt relative to its circumstellar disk is called stellar obliquity. It notes that many solar‑type stars exhibit a wide range of obliquities and that scientists have long wondered how a star’s initial obliquity might influence the planetary system that forms around it, including the potential habitability of those planets.
summary: Stellar obliquity refers to a star's axial tilt relative to its circumstellar disk. Researchers have long questioned how a star's initial obliquity affects the planetary system that forms around it.
author: Phys.org

title: Queensland's early storm season spurs focus on disaster preparedness
content:
After an early start to Queensland's storm season, severe storms and flooding have already affected communities across the state.  

In response, attention is once again turning to disaster preparedness and response.
summary: Queensland's storm season has started early, with severe storms and flooding affecting communities across the state. The situation has renewed attention on disaster preparedness and response.
author: Phys.org

title: EU Law Volume Doubles to 47,600 Pages by 2025
content:
A new EU Bureaucracy Index has been released to measure the volume of EU law in force. According to the index, by the end of 2025 the EU’s regulations and directives totaled roughly 47,600 standard pages—an increase of 118 % compared with 2010. The data show that the body of EU law has more than doubled over the past 15 years and continued to expand in 2025.

The index identifies sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law as the main drivers of this growth. These areas have seen the most significant additions to the EU legal framework, contributing to the record‑high volume of binding legislation.
summary: The EU Bureaucracy Index shows EU regulations and directives in force reached about 47,600 standard pages by the end of 2025, an increase of 118% from 2010. The growth is driven mainly by sanctions regulations and new rules in environmental, consumer, and health law.
author: Phys.org

title: Atom-sized black holes could force entire stars to explode
content: The early universe may have generated minuscule black holes that could still exist today. If present, these atom-sized objects might consume stars from the inside or trigger their complete explosion.
summary: The early universe may have produced minuscule black holes that could still exist today. If present, these objects could devour stars from the inside or blow them up entirely.
author: New Scientist

title: Claude AI and Levent Alpöge claim proof of Riemann hypothesis
content: Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven. That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof. Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist
summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced that he and Claude AI had proved the Riemann hypothesis. The claim, reported by Guardian columnist Rafael Behr, marks a shift from conjecture to proof in mathematics.
author: Guardian Science

title: Dolphins in large social groups live longer, Australian study finds
content:
Australian researchers have found that Indo‑Pacific bottlenose dolphins that maintain active social lives and large friendship groups tend to live longer. Decades of data collected at WA’s Shark Bay support the finding.

The study, published in PLOS Biology, notes that dolphins can live for more than 50 years and that group size increases during youth and early adulthood before declining toward the end of life. The research suggests that social engagement may influence longevity in these marine mammals.

Readers can sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter.
summary: Decades of data from WA’s Shark Bay indicate that Indo‑Pacific bottlenose dolphins that socialise in large, consistently sized groups live longer. The PLOS Biology study found that group size increases during youth and early adulthood before declining toward the end of life, and that these dolphins can live more than 50 years.
author: Guardian Science

title: Research shows tide height can differ by a metre across a beach, aiding local flood forecasts
content:
New research shows that tidal height can vary by as much as a metre across the length of a single beach. This variation is invisible when the sea appears level, but it has significant implications for flood predictions and for identifying locations most vulnerable to storm surges.

Until now, tidal information has come mainly from tide gauges, which record levels at a single point, and from satellite radar, which averages data over tens of kilometres. By analysing these differences in tidal height across beaches, scientists suggest that more localised tide and flood forecasts could be developed, improving accuracy for communities at risk.
summary: Researchers found that tidal height can vary by as much as a metre across the length of a single beach. The finding could enable more localized tide and flood forecasts, improving predictions of storm‑surge vulnerability compared with traditional tide gauges and satellite radar averages.
author: Guardian Science

title: Landsat 8 image shows Georgia’s southwest pecan orchards on Oct 23 2026
content:
Georgia’s Pecan Belt

The Earth Observatory’s “Pecan Belt” image was captured by the Operational Land Imager (OLI) aboard NASA’s Landsat 8 satellite on October 23, 2026. The photograph shows the area around Albany, in Dougherty County, during the typical pecan harvest season that runs from October through December. The image is part of the Cropland Data Layer, an annual map of crop types across the contiguous United States produced by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS). The 2025 edition of that map places pecan groves along the Flint River within the Coastal Plain.

Pecans (Carya illinoinensis) are a species of hickory in the walnut family that grow on trees native to North America. The United States grows most of its pecans in Georgia, a state that has historically led the nation in production. The southwest region of Georgia, particularly the area around Albany, is a key cultivation zone. Pecan trees require abundant water and thrive in the well‑drained sandy soils that sit above the Floridan aquifer system, which growers can tap for irrigation.

The history of pecan production in Georgia dates back to the late 1800s, when the state had less than 100 acres of orchards. In the early 1900s, Dougherty and Mitchell counties experienced a pecan boom, planting and selling thousands of acres to investors. By the end of the 1950s, Georgia produced over 17 million pounds of pecans, according to the 1959 agricultural census, and had become the leading producer in the country. In recent decades, other states such as New Mexico and Texas have expanded their production, but Georgia’s output has remained strong.

Georgia’s pecan industry has faced challenges from natural disasters. Hurricane Michael damaged orchards in October 2018, and Hurricane Helene caused additional damage when it swept inland in September 2024. Despite these setbacks, USDA data show that the state’s production has topped 100 million pounds in each of the past three years (2023‑2025). In 2026, a wet summer in parts of the state helped a fungal disease known as scab take hold, producing brown spots on pecan twigs, leaves, and nut shucks. Some growers who were still recovering from Hurricane Helene reported a return of a solid crop.

The image and accompanying story were produced by Lauren Dauphin using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey, with the article written by Kathryn Hansen. The Earth Observatory provides this visual and narrative to highlight the importance of Georgia’s pecan belt within the broader context of U.S. agriculture and the impacts of weather and disease on crop production.
summary: The Operational Land Imager on Landsat 8 captured an image of the area around Albany, Georgia, on October 23 2026, during the pecan harvest season. The photograph highlights pecan groves alongside peanuts, cotton and corn in southwest Georgia’s Dougherty County, a historic pecan‑producing region.

title: NASA’s SPHEREx Satellite Reveals Milky Way Center Through Dust
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 25 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech SPHEREx; data from NASA/IPAC IRSA. Processing: The Bright Nobles (Muhammet Mücahit Soylu, Serdar Aydın, Furkan Küpeli), ChronosphereX (chronospherex. Com). SPHEREx Seeing Through Dust Explanation: What is blocking the center of the Milky Way? During its 13 billion years, our Milky Way has collected a lot of dust. In contrast to the skin cells, dirt, pollen, and other debris that make up the dust behind your couch, cosmic dust is hundreds of times smaller and made of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released into space when a star dies. Today’s video shows infrared light from the Milky Way’s center gathered by NASA’s SPHEREx satellite. Each false color in the video corresponds to the infrared color associated with the wavelength shown in the top left. In the near-infrared, like 1.2 microns, light gets absorbed and scatters off of dust particles. SPHEREx then sees the Galactic Center almost entirely blocked by clouds of dust. In the mid-infrared, though, light is able to pierce through the dust and reach SPHEREx. This is similar to, but not exactly, why sunsets are red! summary: NASA’s SPHEREx satellite captured infrared images of the Milky Way’s center, showing that near‑infrared light is blocked by dust while mid‑infrared light can penetrate it. The video explains that cosmic dust, composed of tiny compounds of oxygen, carbon, and other elements released when stars die, blocks near‑infrared light but allows mid‑infrared light to pass.

title: AI-driven surge in public records requests strains small towns and prompts new state limits
content: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy. Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.” Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget. As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent. Transparency, monetized The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town. This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc.” Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says. SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies. The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors. Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.” While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites. But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment. The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices. In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell. In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year. The AI detection problem It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records. In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year. While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude. On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.” As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.” Everything’s on the table Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing. Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.” Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent. Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments. Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix. As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”
summary: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer.

title: Tidal to delete 27 million AI‑generated tracks and ban fully AI music
content:
Tidal announced that it will completely ban music that is fully generated by artificial intelligence. The company said it will delete all 27 million tracks currently labeled as AI on December 9, noting that those tracks represent about 6.3 percent of its total catalog. Tidal’s statement adds that 96 percent of the AI‑labeled tracks received zero plays in the previous 90 days, so the removal is expected to have essentially no negative impact on listeners.

The ban follows a policy introduced in July 2026 that required labeling and demonetizing songs created entirely with AI. Despite that measure, Tidal reported that AI‑generated uploads continued to rise, accounting for 43 percent of new uploads over the past 90 days and reaching 60 percent on November 6. The new rule clarifies that artists may still employ AI tools provided the final product includes human elements.
summary: Tidal announced it will fully ban music that is completely created by AI and will delete all 27 million AI‑labeled tracks from its catalog on December 9. The company said the removal will have little impact because 96 percent of those tracks received zero plays in the prior 90 days.

title: Tidal bans 100% AI-generated music, aims to delete over 27 million tracks
content: Streaming service says 43% of uploads to platform in past 90 days were made entirely by artificial intelligence The music streaming service Tidal has announced it will ban entirely AI-generated music from its platform and remove millions of songs, saying AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans”. “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” the company announced on Tuesday.
summary: Tidal announced it will ban any music that is 100% AI‑generated and will remove all such tracks from its catalog. The service said AI‑made uploads made up 43% of uploads in the past 90 days and it plans to delete more than 27 million tracks.

title: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson uses AI to draft Molly Meldrum tribute
content:
Anna Spargo‑Ryan recounts asking an artificial‑intelligence system whether it was acceptable to use AI for writing an obituary, noting that the response she received was unexpected. She reflects on her own experience composing a eulogy for her 101‑year‑old grandmother, describing the task as “a writer’s dream” and emphasizing how personal and detailed the tribute became.

The article also points out that the Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team produced a tribute to music‑industry figure Molly Meldrum using AI. Spargo‑Ryan imagines the process as a quick input of Meldrum’s name into the Claude AI system while the rest of the team stepped away for coffee, suggesting the final tribute was generated without direct human drafting. The piece highlights the growing role of AI in creating public memorials.
summary: Jess Wilson’s team generated a tribute to music legend Molly Meldrum using artificial intelligence. They entered Meldrum’s name into the AI tool Claude while staff fetched coffee.
author: Guardian Technology

title: China-linked battery projects may receive UK state subsidies despite security concerns
content: China-made lithium-ion batteries, which are relatively low-cost, dominate Ofgem project shortlist A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears over the risk of foreign interference they could pose to Europe’s energy systems. Ofgem, Great Britain’s energy regulator, published a provisional shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme in June. The list was dominated by projects relying on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software.
summary: A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears of foreign interference risks to Europe’s energy systems. Ofgem’s provisional June shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme was dominated by lithium‑ion battery projects typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Huawei convicted of stealing US trade secrets in Brooklyn federal trial
content: US attorney general Todd Blanche says ‘No person or company is above the law’ after tech giant found guilty on 10 of 12 criminal counts Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted on Tuesday in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it stole ⁠trade secrets from US companies and deceived banks about ⁠its business in Iran. Huawei, the world’s leading telecom equipment manufacturer, was found guilty by a ​federal jury in Brooklyn of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the US. It was found not guilty of racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging it had acted as a criminal enterprise.
summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts, including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the United States, while acquitting it of racketeering conspiracy. US attorney general Todd Blanche said ‘No person or company is above the law’ after the verdict.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta employees warn AI moderation push may cause large‑scale mistakes
content: Meta employees have voiced concerns that the company’s move to replace human moderators with artificial‑intelligence systems could generate large‑scale errors. Several staff members say the rapid speed of algorithmic decisions increases the risk of mistakes that might have sweeping political consequences. Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has been testing AI‑driven moderation since 2017, when it first deployed the technology to filter violent extremist content. The insiders’ remarks highlight internal unease about the broader impact of the AI‑centric approach.
summary: Meta employees say the company's move to replace human moderators with artificial intelligence could produce large‑scale mistakes and political fallout. The firm has been testing AI‑driven moderation since 2017, initially to filter violent extremist content on Facebook and Instagram.
author: Guardian Technology

content: Thousands of teachers marched in Santiago as part of a nationwide strike protesting proposed budget cuts to public and higher education in Chile. During the demonstrations, some protesters came into conflict with police.

title: Haitians praise Salvadoran president's tough anti‑gang tactics
content:
Haitians are praising the Bukele method, describing it as the Salvadoran president’s “shoot first, ask questions later” approach to gangs that have overrun the country for the past six years. Citizens of the Americas’ poorest nation are cheering the strong‑arm tactics that have been implemented in El Salvador.

The question remains whether the police force deployed in Haiti can restore law and order. This effort is part of a decades‑long list of initiatives by the international community to support the nation.
summary: Haitians are hailing the Salvadoran president’s “shoot first, ask questions later” method of dealing with gangs that have overrun their country for six years. The piece asks whether a police force deployed under this approach can restore law and order amid a decades‑long list of international efforts to support Haiti.

title: NATO chief says alliance will defend against space threats as Russia eyes nuclear satellite
content: NATO chief Mark Rutte said Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Jennie Shin, Dafydd Townley, Senior Teaching Fellow in International Security at the University of Portsmouth, says that the alleged plan would be "foolhardy because the impact would be indiscriminate, they wouldn't be able to choose only Western or non-Russian satellites".
summary: NATO chief says alliance will defend against space threats as Russia eyes nuclear satellite.

content:

title: Blade Runner 2099' Producers Discuss Architectural Easter Eggs and Franchise Continuity
content: Prime Video's new " Blade Runner 2099 " series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising. This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, " Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve. Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, " Blade Runner 2099 " hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions. Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret. (Image credit: Alberto Rodriguez/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images) We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel. "When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over." "Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo. "We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion." (Image credit: Prime Video) Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced. "Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey." With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of " Blade Runner 2099's " 8-episode season. Michelle Yeoh stars as a dying replicant in "Blade Runner 2099" (Image credit: Prime Video) "You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner. "There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.” "Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.
summary: Prime Video's new " Blade Runner 2099 " series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head.
author: Space.com

title: SpaceX launches USSF-266 classified mission from Vandenberg for Space Force
content:
SpaceX carried out a classified launch for the U.S. Space Force on November 24, sending the USSF‑266 mission into low Earth orbit from Vandenberg Space Force Base’s Space Launch Complex‑4E. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off at 11:08 a.m. local time (1508 GMT) carrying an undisclosed payload. The launch marked the fourth SpaceX flight for the Space Force that month and the fifth U.S. national‑security launch in the preceding two weeks, as the Space Force works to broaden its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9’s first‑stage booster separated from the upper stage, which continued toward orbit with the classified payload. The booster then returned to the Pacific Ocean, landing on SpaceX’s “Of Course I Still Love You” droneship roughly eight and a half minutes after launch. This flight was the 29th for booster B1081, which has previously launched NASA’s Crew‑7 mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two earlier classified Space Force missions (USSF‑153 and USSF‑481), and 16 Starlink missions.

While SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF‑266 carries its Starshield satellites—adapted from the Starlink constellation for national‑security uses—previous classified launches have sparked speculation about such deployments. USSF‑266 follows three other Space Force missions launched from Vandenberg earlier this month (USSF‑432 on Nov. 6, USSF‑627 on Nov. 11, and USSF‑317 on Nov. 20) and a National Reconnaissance Office launch, NROL‑136, on Nov. 22, all of which also used Falcon 9 rockets with undisclosed payloads.
summary: SpaceX launches USSF-266 classified mission from Vandenberg for Space Force.

title: Gukesh escapes time crisis to draw world chess championship opener with Sindarov
content: Opening game ends in draw by repetition Defending champion plays white in Game 2 Read our move-by-move report of Game 1 Sindarov: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’ Indian chess star Gukesh Dommaraju held off Javokhir Sindarov amid a mounting time crisis on Tuesday, drawing the opening game of their eagerly awaited $2.5m world title match in 38 moves at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in the picturesque Geneva suburb of Cologny. After spending more than 36 minutes on a single move and much of the afternoon racing against the clock, the defending champion said the time he invested early helped him play faster as a drawish position sharpened and his minutes dwindled opposite the in-form Uzbek challenger. “When I got into the time trouble, I’d already thought about the next few moves,” Gukesh said. “And then the moves after that were pretty easy.”

title: Gul scores as Galatasaray beat Aston Villa in Champions League
content:
Aston Villa suffered a Champions League defeat at Galatasaray in Istanbul, marking their sixth consecutive match without a win in all competitions. The Turkish hosts secured the victory with a 77th-minute goal from substitute Deniz Gul, who was the game’s first effort on target. Gul sustained a facial injury during the match, requiring a bandage after receiving a boot to the face from Nicolas Jackson.

The loss was Villa’s third trip to Istanbul this calendar year, contrasting sharply with their previous visits to Fenerbahce in January and their Europa League triumph at Besiktas Park in May. Manager Unai Emery noted that the poor pitch conditions, which began deteriorating during warm-ups, were equal for both teams. Despite John McGinn’s frustration with the surface after a through ball went awry, the article states that no one from Villa could blame the defeat on the playing conditions. Galatasaray maintained their strong home form, while Villa made four changes from their recent stalemate with Sunderland.
summary: Deniz Gul scored the only goal in the 77th minute to secure a victory for Galatasaray over Aston Villa. This result extended Aston Villa's winless run to six matches in all competitions.

title: Rayan Cherki equalizer denies Manchester City win against Napoli
content:

The match featured a debut for City’s new rust-colored kit, though the performance largely reflected a familiar frustration before the home side shook off their torpor in the closing stages.

Rayan Cherki provided a crucial equalizer, scoring with an angled shot that passed Vanja Milinkovic-Savic after an otherwise fruitless evening of effort. This goal denied Napoli a victory and ended the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne.

Although Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A, were described as lacking their previous intensity, City’s inability to maintain a lead meant they could not secure a win. The match served as a snapshot of the team’s autumn challenges, with the final scoreline offering only partial relief from their defensive vulnerabilities.
summary: Rayan Cherki scored an equalizer to prevent Manchester City from defeating Napoli in a match that highlighted the visitors' ongoing struggles. The result ended the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne, who played in the game.

title: England coastal areas to receive over £11m for 12 council‑led projects
content:

The money will be distributed across 12 council‑led projects aimed at detecting coastal change earlier and assisting local planning.

Among the supported schemes are laser‑equipped drone surveys, sand dune restoration, and the relocation of roads inland. These initiatives are intended to give seaside communities tools to monitor erosion and to prepare for its impacts.
summary: More than £11 million will be shared among 12 council‑led projects in England’s seaside communities. The projects, such as laser‑equipped drone surveys, sand dune restoration and moving roads inland, aim to detect coastal change earlier and help communities plan for rising seas and accelerated erosion.
author: Guardian Environment

title: 120 climate scientists urge US lawmakers to reject Baaja permitting bill
content:
More than 120 climate scientists have signed an open letter urging US House members to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, commonly known as Baaja. The researchers, who include Earth and social sciences experts, stated they have “deep concern” that the legislation weakens environmental laws. They further argued that the bill locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and results in only minor reductions to planet-heating emissions.

The letter warns that Baaja, which is intended to expedite energy and infrastructure projects, will cause irreversible climate harm. This call for a "no" vote comes amid a growing backlash against the sweeping permitting bill, which aims to accelerate the construction of energy projects, datacenters, and other infrastructure.
summary: More than 120 climate scientists sent an open letter to House members urging them to vote against the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The researchers stated that the bill weakens environmental laws and locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse.
author: Guardian Environment

title: California king tides flood San Francisco low-lying areas
content:
California is experiencing record-high November tides that have caused flooding in low-lying areas along the coast. In San Francisco, flood waters rushed over the bayfront Embarcadero in the city’s tourist district, while flooded roadways were reported from San Rafael to Redwood Shores. These events occurred despite clear skies, and monthly tide records were set across the city, with some expected to reach even higher levels tomorrow.

The extreme tides have also prompted an evacuation of one community in northern California. Local residents and media outlets shared images documenting the widespread impact of the water on roadways and public spaces.
summary: Record-high November tides caused flooding in San Francisco's Embarcadero and other coastal areas. One community in northern California was evacuated due to the high water levels.
author: Guardian Environment

title: b/tsDMARD use patterns in rheumatoid arthritis linked to genetic associations
content: A study published online Nov. 20 in Arthritis & Rheumatology reports that common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) use exist among patients with rheumatoid arthritis. The research indicates that these specific usage patterns are associated with underlying genetic associations.
summary: A study found that common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic DMARD use among rheumatoid arthritis patients are associated with underlying genetic factors. The research was published online in Arthritis & Rheumatology on November 20.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer
content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with locally advanced or metastatic ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer who have received prior treatment. The approval was granted to Nuvalent and GSK.
summary: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study links inflammatory bowel disease to higher cirrhosis risk
content: A study published in Sage Open Chronic Diseases reports that inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), particularly ulcerative colitis, is associated with an increased risk for a cirrhosis diagnosis.
summary: A study published in Sage Open Chronic Diseases found that inflammatory bowel disease is associated with an increased risk for cirrhosis diagnosis. The research specifically noted that this link is especially prominent in patients with ulcerative colitis.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FDA approves bezuclastinib plus sunitinib for second-line GIST therapy
content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved the combination of bezuclastinib and sunitinib as a second-line therapy for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) following first-line imatinib treatment. This decision was based on phase 3 PEAK study data led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, which demonstrated that the combination outperformed standard sunitinib monotherapy.
summary: The FDA approved the combination of bezuclastinib and sunitinib as a second-line treatment for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors. This decision follows the phase 3 PEAK study, which demonstrated that the combination outperformed sunitinib alone after first-line imatinib treatment.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Prior Authorization Limits Increase Buprenorphine Use in Medicaid States with Barriers
content: A new study led by University of Michigan researchers found that state laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid. This association was observed only in states where such prior authorization requirements had frequently acted as barriers to access.
summary: State laws limiting prior authorization for opioid use disorder medications were linked to higher buprenorphine use in Medicaid. The effect was seen only in states where prior authorization requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a University of Michigan study.
author: Medical Xpress

title: England Leads 31-Country Study with Largest Socioeconomic Frailty Gap
content: A recent study of 31 countries found that older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience higher levels of frailty. Among the nations examined, England displayed the widest gap in frailty between socioeconomic groups.
summary: Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty. England shows the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects
content: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. Researchers note that tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing. Yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.
summary: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff for code of conduct violations
content:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang apologized to employees on Tuesday, saying he had caused “tumult” at the company. In a livestream reviewed by the New York Times, Huang acknowledged that he violated Nvidia’s code of conduct by engaging in extramarital affairs, describing his actions as “terrible mistakes” that hurt his wife Lori, his children and the staff.

He also rejected media reports that former President Donald Trump played a role in Huang’s return to the chief‑executive post, stating that those claims were inaccurate.
summary: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, apologized to employees, saying he made terrible mistakes and hurt his family and staff. He acknowledged violating the company’s code of conduct by having extramarital affairs and denied that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.
author: Guardian Business

title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
content:
Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea. Madin utilized specimens and data collected by MBARI’s advanced underwater robots to document the animal, which researchers had first observed in the deep waters of Monterey Bay more than 20 years ago.

Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. The new publication provides a comprehensive account of this previously unfamiliar species, highlighting its unique adaptation to deep-sea habitats.
summary: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay.
author: Phys.org

title: Laser light maps electron accumulation in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
content:
A multi-institutional team in Japan has demonstrated that shining laser light on stacked semiconductors reveals where electrons accumulate within atomically thin stacks. While stacking these materials, which power devices such as phones and computers, allows for quicker signal movement with less energy, the specific mechanisms of electron movement had remained unclear. This optical approach provides a method to visualize these internal processes.

The researchers stated that this technique could inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics. By elucidating how electrons move within the semiconductor stacks, the study offers new insights into optimizing the performance of next-generation electronic components.
summary: Stacking semiconductors enables quicker signal movement with less energy. A multi‑institutional team in Japan used laser light to reveal how electrons move in the stack, a method that could help develop more efficient, low‑power electronics, the researchers said.
author: Phys.org

title: Quantum ingenuity can sidestep limits of conventional chips—while using commercially accessible components
content: Computers have steadily become faster and more powerful over the past decades. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, proposes a dramatic new leap forward that would be driven by the quantum properties of light.
summary: For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists Achieve First Total Synthesis of Antitussive Alkaloid Neotuberostemonine
content:
Researchers have accomplished the first total synthesis of neotuberostemonine, a complex plant‑derived alkaloid noted for its antitussive activity. The breakthrough also included the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L, compounds that had remained elusive for nearly three decades.

The study further revealed that the nearly planar geometry of the alkaloids’ nitrogen atoms contributes to their oxidative instability. These insights provide new synthetic strategies for natural‑product chemistry and may inform future drug‑discovery efforts.
summary: Researchers have achieved the first total synthesis of the plant-derived alkaloid Neotuberostemonine, known for its antitussive activity. The study also synthesized neostenine, proposed the structure of tuberostemonine L, and showed that the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the alkaloids' oxidative instability, providing new synthetic strategies.
author: Phys.org

title: Depression Linked to Tau Protein Accumulation in Older Adults
content:
Scientists have found a link between accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and worsening depressive symptoms in older adults. This association was observed in individuals who still possessed normal memory and thinking abilities. The research indicates that the rate of tau buildup in the brain corresponds with the speed at which depressive symptoms increase.

These findings suggest that mood changes may serve as an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease, potentially emerging before any cognitive decline is detected.
summary: Scientists found that accumulating tau protein was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in older adults with normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up, the faster depressive symptoms increased, indicating mood changes may appear before cognitive decline.
author: Science Daily

title: New materials crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures using internal energy
content: Scientists have created materials that can crawl, walk, and dig by using their own internal energy, offering a potential foundation for autonomous soft robots. In testing, they found that increasing the activity of individual components can paradoxically reduce the overall responsiveness of the material, challenging a long‑standing engineering principle.
summary: Scientists have developed materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially enabling new autonomous soft robots. They also found that increasing component activity can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive.
author: Science Daily

title: MIT scientists discover primordial black holes could devour stars and trigger explosions
content: MIT scientists report that tiny black holes from the Big Bang could slowly consume stars from the inside, leading to spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these events may confirm the existence of primordial black holes and help resolve the mystery of dark matter.
summary: MIT scientists discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.
author: Science Daily

title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
content: A new analysis proposes that Earth’s transition from an oxygen-poor environment to one supporting complex life occurred in three distinct atmospheric stages. The study indicates that the oceans lagged behind this atmospheric accumulation, potentially taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to reach comparable oxygen levels.
summary: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history.
author: Science Daily

title: Nasal drops restore memory and halt Alzheimer’s-like decline in mice
content:
A new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory in aging mice and prevented severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate the production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory.

The treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a distinct approach to combating cognitive decline.
summary: The nasal treatment restored youthful learning and memory in aging mice and prevented severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. It works by stimulating production of a brain‑protecting protein and preserves brain function without removing Alzheimer’s plaques.
author: Science Daily

title: Beaver Moon Illuminates Night Sky Worldwide on November 24
content: The largest supermoon of the year, the beaver moon, illuminated the night sky on 24 November, delighting skywatchers worldwide. Images from locations ranging from Salzburg to Srinagar showcase some of the best views of the event.
summary: The largest supermoon of the year, known as the beaver moon, illuminated the night sky on 24 November. Skywatchers from Salzburg to Srinagar enjoyed the view, as shown in the accompanying pictures.
author: Guardian Science

title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission to Deliver 11,000 Pounds of Supplies to ISS
content:
NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 (CRS‑25) mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station (ISS). The cargo is carried on the company’s Cygnus XL spacecraft, the larger, more cargo‑capable version of its solar‑powered spacecraft. Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

After launch, the Cygnus XL will rendezvous with the ISS. Astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will be on duty during the spacecraft’s approach. Watkins will operate the Canadarm2 robotic arm, while Delaney will monitor the arrival of Cygnus. Once captured, ground controllers will robotically install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth‑facing port for cargo unloading.

The cargo package includes crew supplies such as food, blankets, hatch seal covers, a modified toilet pretreat hose, Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer spacewalk tools, and batteries for the Anomaly Gas Analyzer. In addition to these items, Cygnus will carry several experiments aimed at advancing medical research and life‑support technologies for future missions. The experiments include Cardinal Muscle 2.0, which tests potential therapeutics on engineered muscle tissue to address age‑related muscle loss; DNA Nano Therapeutics‑Mission 2, which manufactures DNA‑inspired nanoparticles for targeted drug delivery; the Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES), which monitors radiation in habitable spacecraft environments; Encapsulate‑1, which grows patient‑derived tumor samples to study metastasis; and OHALO III, a plant‑growth facility that validates water delivery and crop production for long‑duration missions. A technology demonstration, IN‑Space (JOINS), will perform autonomous robotic welding in the Bishop Airlock, testing laser beam welding and friction stir welding on aluminum and stainless‑steel.

The mission’s payload and experiments support NASA’s ongoing research into health, safety, and life‑support systems for crewed spaceflight. For more information on NASA’s work in low Earth orbit, visit https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station.
summary: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.
author: NASA News

title: Kilonova Catcher lets amateur astronomers help track neutron‑star collisions
content:
NASA’s Kilonova Catcher invites amateur astronomers to help track some of the universe’s most fleeting fireworks. When two neutron stars collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These events, which fade within days, are responsible for forging much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Because no single observatory can monitor the entire sky, the Kilonova Catcher network relies on volunteers with telescopes and cameras to respond quickly to alerts from gravitational‑wave detectors or space telescopes.

The network operates as a rapid‑response system. When a gravitational‑wave detector or a space‑based instrument issues an alert, participants point their telescopes at the indicated sky region to locate and follow the fading light. The same system also follows up on gamma‑ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and other short‑lived cosmic events whenever an opportunity arises.

More than 150 members across several continents have joined the effort. Their observations have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the real‑time system scientists use to exchange discoveries. Volunteers’ data have been credited as authors in peer‑reviewed scientific papers. In addition, Kilonova Catcher participants joined NASA’s lunar Impact Flash! Project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light produced when meteoroids strike the Moon.

The project is preparing to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s forthcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. “Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational‑wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.”

The project is co‑led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Turpin noted, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.” To join, visit https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/ or email kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone with access to a telescope equipped with a camera can participate.
summary: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science Amateur Astronomer? Be a… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars.
author: NASA News
